notes.title: Mapping Modern Images onto Older Maps and Drawings
body: We’d been working on synthesising historical stories about the arrival of the French, the temples that were documented in this town at the time, the maps in which we see them, and so on. In the process we came across temple images of those times, drawn by travellers and others who found Pondicherie such a curiosity. One was an image of what looked to us like it must have been the Perumal Koyil, so we took a break to go ask about this. But, no this was a non-starter: Dinesh Bhattacharya at main Perumal Sannathi said the gopuram was constructed in 1998 and that the Sivan koyil gopuram is older. So what’s in our image cannot possibly be the Perumal Koyil. All these colonial era images are so much more about typecasting than they are about identifying monuments at specific places.

notes.title: The Start of the Utsavam for Periyalvar
body: This starts today and will continue for 10 days. The process is usually this: morning thirumanjanam for the Alvar utsavam. Alankara is done, and in the evening the adhyapakas recite specific verses from the Alvar’s repertoire (mangalasasanam). This is followed by an ul-purappadu, and sattrumurai. On the last day, there may be variations – Perumal gets an abhishekam, there is an ethir sevai, a special alankara etc. We’re not there for the beginning though.

notes.title: Waking Up Siva
body: The intent is to go to the Chetty koyil, but it’s not open at 6am, nothing is happening at Kannika, so we wind up at Vedapuriswara. We’re wandering the Nandavanam with the gardener when the sounds call us back to the temple. Quite the process. It’s Friday but the Ambal figure stays in the Palliyarai unlike in the Chetty temple (She comes out on Mondays at this temple). All done by the two younger priests, who seem to do a lot of grunt work and speak very little to anyone. There’s a group of about 15 who sing regularly, a man to play the damaru and sound the conch, someone to play the murasu for siva and another for Ambal (though he is less adept).

The song set appears to be standard offerings from Manikkavasagar Thirupalliyezhucchi, Pancha Puranam, plus some smatterings from Abhirami Anthathi, Thiruppugazh (including Kaithala niraikani) and so on. Abhirami stotram sung by the inimitable Lalitamma whose voice and projection are like gold. An older man leads the “Om nama sivaya sivaya nama om”.
Lalitamma sings two songs composed by Abhirami Bhattar (the first one Arasoo Swamy sings beautifully also, but more on that later):

list: First Abirami Ammai Padhigam of three such sets, this is the most well-known.

body: கலையாத கல்வியும் குறையாத வயதும் ஓர் கபடு வாராத நட்பும்
கன்றாத வளமையும் குன்றாத இளமையும் கழுபிணியிலாத உடலும்
சலியாத மனமும் அன்பகலாத மனைவியும் தவறாத சந்தானமும்
தாழாத கீர்த்தியும் மாறாத வார்த்தையும் தடைகள் வாராத கொடையும்
தொலையாத நிதியமும் கோணாத கோலும் ஒரு துன்பமில்லாத வாழ்வும்
துய்ய நின் பாதத்தில் அன்பும் உதவி பெரிய தொண்டரொடு கூட்டு கண்டாய்!
அலையாழி அறிதுயிலும் மாயனது தங்கையே! ஆதிகடவூரின் வாழ்வே!
அமுதீசர் ஒருபாகம் அகலாத சுகபாணி! அருள்வாமி! அபிராமியே!

kalaiyāda kalviyum kuṟaiyāda vayadum ōr kapaḍu vārāda naṭpumkaṉṟāda vaḷamaiyum kuṉṟāda iḷamaiyum kazhu piṇiyilāda uḍalumcaliyāda maṉamum aṉbu agalāda maṉaiviyum tavaṟāda santāṉamumtāḻāda kīrttiyum māṟāda vārttaiyum taḍaigaḷ vārāda koḍaiyumtolaiyāda nidhiyamum kōṇāda kōlum oru tuṉpam illāda vāḻvumtuyya nin pādattiṉil aṉbum udavi periya toṇḍaroḍu kūṭṭu kaṇḍāy!alaiyāḻi aṟituyilum māyaṉadu taṅgaiyē! ādikaḍavūriṉ vāḻvē!amudīśar ōrupāgam agalāda sugapāṇi! aruḷvāmi! abirāmiyē!
Knowledge that you do not forget, age that does not diminish,
A friendship that does not diminish, A wealth that does not deteriorate ,
A youth that does not diminish, a body that is free from all diseases,
A mind that does not get bored, a wife whose love never diminishes,
A progeny that is regular, a fame that never diminishes,
The promises that are never broken, the charity that never has a road block,
A treasure that is never is lost, a government which is always just,
And a life which never has any sorrow and love towards your very pure divine feet,
And if you also bless me with the company of your great devotees,
Oh sister who sleeps on a leaf floating in the sea, Oh life of ancient Kadavur,
Oh Goddess who does not move away from one side of Lord Shiva,
Oh Goddess who holds a parrot, Please grant me all these Abhirami
[Translation by P.R. Ramachander)]
பூத்தவளே புவனம் பதினான்கையும் பூத்தவண்ணம்
காத்தவளே பின் கரந்தவளே கறைகண்டனுக்கு
மூத்தவளே என்றும் மூவா முகுந்தற்கு இளையவளே
மாத்தவளே உன்னை அன்றி மற்றோர் தெய்வம் வந்திப்பதே
O You who brought into being all the fourteen worlds and brought them into bloom!
O You who preserved, then withdrew and concealed them;
O Eternal Mother–
elder to Him whose neck is stained blue,
younger to the ever-youthful Mukunda,
O Peerless Mother–
embodiment of supreme penance!
Other than You, whom else could I worship?

This is the 13th verse of the Abhirami Anthathi, a collection of 100 devotional Tamil hymns dedicated to Goddess Abhirami at the Amirthakadeswarar Temple in Thirukkadaiyur. Composed by the saint Abhirami Bhattar.

notes.title: Twin Pujas on the First Friday of Each New Tamil Month
body: We both went – milkman brings the cow and this time a calf. Puja consists of alankaram for the cow and calf, then priest chants while every one present feeds them both bananas, agathi leaves, and then places flowers on them – a number of pradakshinas, which everyone performs. Then the cow and calf are led around the temple once, and out the door. There they wait patiently, are fed some aval pori, the day’s prasadam (kesari, mercifully, not thairsaadam), and the man milks the cow. This milk is quickly boiled and offered to Vasavi Kannika, with a little jaggery added, then to us all. The cow herd leaves, as do we.
Gopuja happens on the first friday of every tamil month, we’re told, if the Iyer is busy it may become the 2nd Friday.

Deepa goes back in the evening, 630. Just in time for the Mahalakshmi puja which is an abhishekam for a kutty vinayaka and Lakshmi, set up in the main hall. Milk, turmeric, and what I think is rose water are poured via a conch. Ladies from the community are present, though not all from the start. It’s the Mahila Sangam that does this, and all are ubhayakaras, all are asked by the Iyer to take a sankalpam. No elaneer etc. but other abhishekam is done. After, the alankaram etc. are a simple affair. Statues dressed and lifted into the small golden mandapa that’s set up outside the main shrine, dressed with flowers.

Baskets of flowers are distributed, and 2 plates for those sitting away or on chairs –one with flowers, one to place flowers. Priest chants, women offer flowers. Those closest offer flowers directly onto the deities. This goes on a while.

Then the women sing and chant from a book. There’s some talk of giving gotra names but this doesn’t seem to happen. They say the Ganesha Pancharatnam and Kanakadhara stotram (but of course) and start on something else but by now it’s 8 and I must leave. I speak to the main lady who is obviously a prominent organiser and thank her and offer to send photos as the ladies have been asking me to take some with their phones anyway. She’s very nice and welcoming, asks me to come again and often. She’s busy with the priest breaking coconuts and presumably preparing the day’s tambulam bags or prasadam take-home packets (there are a lot of buckets that come from the madapalli) when I leave.

notes.title: Sivan and Ambal Return to the Palliyarai Together
body: Finally get to see the Palliyarai utsavam here, with both Sivan and Ambal going to the Palliyarai. It all feels a bit abrupt and fast, but the process is roughly the same as in the Sivan Koyil, sans the crowd of bhaktas each playing an instrument or singing a song. There appears to be less of a culture of this at the Chetty Temple.

notes.title: Thirupalliyezhucchi, Redux
body: I went again. Pretty much same-same, but I could absorb and understand it better. Song set included beautiful renditions of Thiruppugazh 110, Yeru mayileri (1328), and Vilayaada odi vaa muruga – by 3 ladies who stayed till the end, the best of whom was Lalitamma.

Also tevaram maybe from this set. Or was it Thiruperunthurai [Thiruvasagam (திருவாசகம்) composed by the saint Manikkavasagar at the Athmanatha Swami Temple (also known as Avudaiyarkoil), most probably, but not sure. Will need to go again to confirm].

notes.title: Perumal’s Preparatory Pujas
body: Arun was there for this, as Deepa wasn’t around. One priest called in from outside for this, along with 3 helpers. With Sridhar Bhattacharya also around, this made 5 total. Yagashala in the usual spot beside the Perumal Koyil. The person deputed to carry the sand collected for Ankurarpana or the seed sprouting is Sridhar Bhattacharya. Milk and water are poured over, there is an aradhanai, and then of course the Vastu purusha effigy is burned and carried outside as part of the Vastu Shanti puja process. THe tiny utsavar of Vishwaksena then has his ul-purappadu.
1030AM: Thirumanjanam
6PM-730PM: Mrtsangrahanam, Ankurarpanam, Vastu Shanti, Sri Vishwaksena ul-purappadu

notes.title: Vasantha Utsavam Begins as Periyalvar Is Still Being Feted
notes.occasion: Periyalvar Utsavam Day 5; Vasanta Utsavam Day 1
body: I (Arun) came here directly from Chetty Koyil. Perumal was already in the Vasantha Mandapam, with nobody looking at him! Rope tied at the first 2 pillars, so you couldn’t really get to him, and there stood a security guard for good measure! All attention at that moment was at the Periyalvar Sannadhi – a large crowd there, perhaps had come for Vasantha Utsavam, but moved to the Alvar Sannadhi because Aradhanai was happening there.

The patrikai announced the following for this and the next 10 days: From Saturday, 20 June 2026, to Tuesday, 30 June 2026, the festival will take place daily. The procession will begin at 7:00 p.m., followed by the Lord's appearance in the Vasantha Maṇḍapam, the uḷḷañcal sēvai (swing service), and the distribution of tīrtham (thirtha prasadha ghosti) and prasādam.

notes.title: The Kodi Gets Raised at the Chetty Perumal Koyil
body: Arun went in the morning, and reported a slow process, but Perumal’s flag was finally raised on the smallish kodi maram. In the evening, we both were there; the priests looked slightly frazzled, clearly dealing with some unease between priests and Ubhayakaras, quickly assuaged by the very skillful manner of Sankara Narayana Chettiar.

Perumal was Mohana that evening, or perhaps it’s better to call this Nachiyar thirukolam as Thathacharya from Perumal Koyil would say, with a veena. Veethi purappadu happened but with a fraction of the interest and fanfare that’s typical of the Perumal koyil.
The day’s schedule:
AM: after 730 & before 9am – Dhvajarohanam, Perumal Vimana veethi purappadu
PM: Hamsa vahana Veethi purappadu Mohana /Nachiyar Thirukolam

notes.title: Out of the Vasanta Mandapam
notes.occasion: Periyalvar Utsavam Day 6; Vasanta Utsavam Day 2
body: Stopped by the Perumal temple, when the Vasanta utsavam was just rounding up. Prasanna remarked we’d got there late! But we got to see the return of Perumal from the Vasanta Mandapam back into the garba griha. Ubhayakaras included Sasikala whom we see often at the Kannika temple, who said her sister in law was the actual ubhayakari, but couldn’t be there so she came in her stead. I believe this was the day when the security guard shooed me away from the Vasanta Mandapam for taking video of Perumal ever so gently swinging and looking mighty grand. I’d like to understand this festival better though. Is it really just a kind of divine pastime? Do the Gods get tired and need such recreation?

notes.title: An All-in-White Nataraja on the Eve of Aani Thirumanjanam
body: AANI UTTHIRAM. Saw the ardhajama puja at the Sivan koyil, and Natarajar in vellai saatthupadi. The koyil Patrikai had announced that “There will be a Vellai Sathupadi (white attire) decoration for the festival deity Lord Nataraja, followed by Deeparadhana (lamp worship ritual) and Ul Purappadu (inner temple procession).” But we missed this, thinking of Aani Utthiram as just the next morning’s event.

notes.title: Perumal as Surya, in a Blaze of Orange
body: We were there for the Surya Prabhai purappadu beginning, Perumal came out into the sun with two large orange kudais shading him. Very bright and cheery and sun-like. In the evening, He’s on the Lion vahana.
Arrangements are made also for the Aani Thirumanjanam abhishekam here, but we only see those as we’ve to get to the Sivan Koyil for the full event this time.
Today’s schedule:
8AM Surya Prabhai, 10AM Thirumanjanam
7PM Simha vahana veethi purappadu

notes.title: A Thirumanjanam to Mark a Cosmic Moment
body: Aani Thirumanjanam is but a moment in a wide cosmic scene—

when the Sun transits through Mithuna ubaya rasi (constellation set), and its placement in Siva’s own Thiruvathirai nakshatram comes into alignment with the movement of the moon into the Sun’s star, Uttiram—
when Siva blessed the Nayanmar Saint Maanikkavasagar with his divine upadesha (instruction or illumination)—
when we mark these movements with Mahabhishekam (sacred bath) for Nataraja, Thillai Koothan, the Great Dancer of Chidambaram—
and yearn for illumination and grace.

Much, much more mundanely, we watched the Thirumanjanam in the outside mandapam at the sivan Koyil, wondering why this particular abhishekam is called a thirumanjanam when none others are. It was done by Kalyana Sundara Gurukkal. We made a video with the footage collected at this scene, largely because the video was actually so much better than the photos! Patrikai had said: “Aani Thirumanjanam Abhishekam (sacred bathing ceremony) for Lord Nataraja will take place, followed by Deeparadhana. At 7:00 PM in the evening, Swami Ul Purappadu (inner temple procession of the Deity) will take place.”

Thirumanjana Abhishekam may be a common phrasing, made to emphasize the complete, grand ritual bathing ceremony, but it feels a touch like a redundancy or (deliberately) an excess of expression. In any case, we were there also for the evening’s purappadu.

notes.title: Into the Vasanta Mandapam
notes.occasion: Periyalvar Utsavam Day 8; Vasanta Utsavam Day 4
body: We went for this, particularly to see the purappadu from the moola sthanam to the Vasanta mandapam. (Periyalvar Utsavam had wound up by then.) Perumal emerges from the moola sthanam and then does the usual circumambulation, stopping at various sannadhis (where the priests take his satari into the other sannadhis, touch them onto heads, shoulders, then brings them out to devotees before finally returning to the waiting Perumal). The final stop is at Hanuman, and then He enters the Vasanta Mandapam, does one round of the place, sits on his swing. The channel is filled with water and floating flowers–a sad simulation of a garden, but still: grand!

notes.title: Mohanavataram Again?
body: Couldn’t figure out why there was a Mohanavatara (Nachiyar Thirukolam) redux, maybe just that this time it’s in a pallaq with a mirror, but there you have it. In the evening Perumal was seated as grandly as a Perum-aal could be, for his evening purappadu on Garuda.
Schedule for the day:
8AM Mohanavataram, Pallaq veethi purappadu, 10AM Thirumanjanam
7PM Garuda Sevai veethi purappadu

notes.title: What’s the Big Deal If Pradosham Falls on a Saturday?
body: When Pradosham falls on a Saturday, it’s a qualitatively different event.

When Trayodashi coincides with Saturday, the observance is called Shani Pradosham. Shani is Saturn of course, and from him the name Shani-varam or Saturday comes. Shani (சனி) is not simply a malefic deity who causes misfortune, but he is a dispenser of justice who compels people to confront the consequences of their karma. Since Pradosham itself is a period when one can worship Siva to wipe away the doshas or faults of past actions, the coming together of Pradosha with Shani-kizhamai is considered doubly auspicious or potent. Incidentally, this is not just a coincidence of Pradosham and Saturday, it is the specific occurrence of tryaodashi during the twilight hour, based on thithi and sunset calculations.

Here’s the process: 330pm abhishekam for Vrushabha and Siva (and Ambal, usually), 6pm ganapati puja, 630pm ul-purappadu with Pradoshanayakar, who circles the main temple three times in its prakaram, first to Vadyam, then to Vedam, and finally to Tamil recitations of Sivapuranam, Tevaram etc. Those last are always a chorus of devotees' voices. At Nandhikeswara the process is much the same, except that Pradosham is always accompanied by Kailaya Vadyam–and that makes for a very different atmosphere. Plus of course, the readings here on second and third rounds are all in Tamil, women are given a chance to carry the deity and there’s a fair bit more dancing!

notes.title: One Perumal, Two Thieves
body: The Vennai thazhi Thirukolam is always a sweet one, Perumal as Krishna with his butter pot, and usually with some special attention to his backside or pin-alankaram as well. But we miss this morning at Chetty Koyil. The evening is on a Kuthirai Vahana, so the alankaram is Thirumangai alvar as usual, but Perumal is accompanied this evening by a far more simply dressed saint, who is also Thirumangai alvar but now in utsavar form. He is presented a sack full of things from the Perumal utsavar (see the story below). Then the two proceed in a ethir sevai, with the alvar facing Perumal as He proceeds to travel his mada veethi processional route.

The story: Kaliyan (Thirumangai Azhwar) performed thadiyaradhanam (offering prasadam to devotees) during his lifetime. At one point, he ran out of wealth and began robbing wealthy merchants and other travellers passing through the forest. Since he was already devoted to serving Sri Vaishnavas, Emperuman, wishing to enlighten Kaliyan fully, assumed the form of a wealthy, newly married Brahmana and travelled through the forest where Kaliyan routinely carried out his robberies.

Kaliyan, wishing to make the most of this opportunity, surrounded Emperuman with his soldiers and began robbing him. Emperuman offered all his ornaments and jewels to Kaliyan. In the end, one small ring on Emperuman's toe proved difficult to remove. Kaliyan bent down, bit it off with his teeth, and forcibly removed it.

Astonished by Kaliyan's bravery, Emperuman exclaimed, “Nam Kaliyano?” (“Are you Kaliyan?”). Kaliyan generally means a great warrior and is synonymous with Kalan, the master of death and controller of time—one who is feared by everyone. Even Emperuman was struck by Kaliyan's valour. After all the ornaments had been removed and packed into a bundle, Kaliyan tried to lift it but found that he could not. He asked Emperuman, who was still dressed as a Brahmana, whether he had performed some mantra or magic that made the bundle impossible to lift. Emperuman acknowledged that he indeed knew a mantra, drew Kaliyan closer, and secretly explained the Thirumanthram (Ashtaksharam) in his ear.

Upon receiving instruction in this divine mantra, Kaliyan was immediately enlightened through the grace of Emperuman. Emperuman then assumed his original form, accompanied by his Nachiyars on Garudazhwar, and blessed the Azhwar with a divine vision.

The Azhwar immediately sang the pasuram “VadinEn vAdi varundhinEn ... Narayana ennum nAmam” (“I suffered and languished in sorrow ... until [I heard] the name Narayana”), which is the first pasuram of Periya Thirumozhi, and went on to sing the other Divya Prabandhams, one after another.
This entire episode is usually enacted at Divya Desams on the day of the Horse Vahanam, which forms part of Brahmotsavam.
The day’s schedule:
8AM Vennai Thaazhi thirukolam, 10AM Thirumanjanam
7PM Kuthirai vahana vedu pari utsavam Veethi purappadu

notes.title: Karaikkal Ammaiyar and the Festival of Ripe Mangoes
body: Organized by the Siruthonda Bhakta Sabhai, this festival is in honor of Karaikkal Ammaiyar. At the Vedapuriswara Koyil, a whole Chariot top is made with mangoes, and mangoes are hung (in unfortunate plastic sleeves) or tied into every possible location. Meanwhile, Karaikkal Ammavar and her utsavar figure get an abhishekam, while a large group of women sing her songs outside the Nayanmar sannadhi. It is unfortunately not very attuned singing, and there’s a noticeable difference for the short time Lalitamma takes the microphone. I borrow one of their booklets and make a PDF out of it for the files. Ammavar meanwhile gets a full alankaram with flower malas and a crown of manoranjitham – she’s almost made to look attractive, and I’m left wondering what a woman who consciously gave up her beauty for the visage of a ghoul in her self-offering to Siva would say about this latter day re-transformation.

There’s a mad crush when the alangarified utsava murti is brought out into the mampazha ther–for the first time, I hear a priest saying “this whole event is all about taking photos and not about seeing Ammavar with bhakti!” We can barely catch a glimpse in between and behind all those with cameras and phones, except via their LCD screens.

The mangani ther goes around the prakaram thrice, and it is quite a sight. Some have organized for water to be poured in places where the stone is heated by the mid-day sun so that priests and devotees can walk without being scorched. The mangani ther stops for a while at the Sivan and Ambal sannadhis before returning. Much later in the evening, when we return – she’s still there in the ther, all alone and unattended. We get our private moments with her then.

In other temples, I’m told, Lord Siva as Bhikshatanar (who comes begging for food and is given one of her mangoes) is taken out on a grand procession. Devotees gather on their rooftops and throw mangani (ripe mangoes) into the streets below for the crowd to catch. Catching these mangoes is believed to bring divine blessings and fulfill wishes. But here the purappadu is inside, so no such throwing happens, thankfully!

notes.title: All the Major Events on Pournami!
body: We made it to the morning’s rathotsavam, or ther vizha. The pulling of a deity in His chariot is always a major event, and the crowds spoke for it. The Chettiar community is welcoming enough that Arun is given a parivattam or small thundu tied around his head, and a pavitram on his right ring finger–so he’s officially now anointed as a participant in the process. It’s a loving gesture of acknowledgment and affirmation. In the afternoon, the theerthavari happened although at the well we were told and not at the sea as it did for Kalathiswara earlier in March/Panguni.

Then finally in the evening, with bowls of vigorously growing sprouts on all corners, the flag finally came down. As it turns out, the Chetty Koyil has a Chandran abhishekam on all Pournami days, so that was going on at the far end, too. It was just getting over as we came for the Dvajarohanam. A small puja would have happened there after alankaram was done, but we have no photos of that.

Way over yonder by Kenikulam where the Chetty Koyil’s Lada Chinnaman lives, an abhishekam must have happened for Her, seeing that that’s their pournami practice, too. It would have been a simple one, just water and maybe milk, but it happened, too.
It was all a lot to pack into a single pournami!
The Day’s schedule:
9-10AM Simha Lakkinathanil Ratharohanam
Noon: Thirumanjanam & Theerthavari
7PM Avarohanam and Kadaporushanam* saattrumurai ul-purappadu
*The Koodapoorushanam (Koodapurasanam / Kadaporushanam) is a specific phase of the Saattrumurai chanted at the conclusion of daily Thiruvaradhanam in the Srivaishnava sampradaya

notes.title: Vasantha Utsavam Concludes with Garuda and Hanuman
body: It is the conclusion of the Vasantha Utsavam today, and we’re going between the final pujas of the Chetty Koyil Perumal Brahmotsavam and this event at the big Perumal temple. Perumal comes out on a wooden Garuda Vahana for a veethi purappadu in the morning (we see Him until the house with the wild pattai pirandai growing out front, from which I take a cutting to root at home). We see the wooden Garuda Vahana for this and perhaps one other purappadu–otherwise, the golden Garuda is for the Brahmotsavam and the silver is for the Periyalvar Utsavam conclusion–otherwise he has no other work, says Thathacharya. In the evening the process repeats, except that this time Perumal is Rama on top of the Hanumantha Vahana.

Mamunigal Thirumanjanam: Today is also Moola nakshatram, so there’s a 1030am event for Sriman Manavala Mamunigal. The patrikai says: “Thirumanjanam (Sacred Bathing Ritual), Sevai (Darsan/Viewing), Satrumarai (Recitation of Sacred Hymns), and Theertha Goshti (Distribution of Sacred Water & Prasadam).”

notes.title: Let the Games Begin!
body: One of the regular ubhayakaras in the Chetty community asks us specifically to come for the morning utsavam, as it’s his ubhayam and he promises it will be like no other. You see Perumal now done with all his Brahmotsavam responsibilities apparently decides to go out for a night on the town, during which he marries (with Mahalakshmi’s permission) the Lady of Uraiyur. When he finally returns home and tries to sneak back indoors, Thayar shuts the door in his face, for she cannot take what she takes to be his philandering. Perumal faces a shut door, and what follows is a ritual enactment of a praṇaya-kalaha, a lovers’ quarrel. When Thayar admits Perumal, He tries to justify his red eyes, scratch marks on his body and his tiredness by saying he was out hunting, but Thayar isn’t falling for his usual charms. Mattaiyadi (மட்டையடி) happens here: literally, a blow with a fibrous stalk or husk; here it refers to the ritual throwing of banana-stem strips at the Lord's palanquin. Some temple folks (us included) take sides. Those for Thayar are the Talattār, those for Perumal are the Toṇḍukulaṭṭār. Finally, Nammazhvar comes to the rescue with consolations and arguments that make Thayar’s heart melt…

All this is ritually enacted by the Bhattacharyas, via a recitation of the “Mattaiyadi puranam” .. but the priests need to be more active and youthful animators to make such an utsavam come to real life, while this one was more entertaining in concept than in execution. Nonetheless, it brought home to us the prospects of “ritual theatre” so to speak, and put us in mind of the various Laksmi Samvadams or sacred dialogues in which such themes as the natures of these divine husbands can be playfully, wittily, and philosophically tossed around.

This is followed by a dwadasha kalasha thirumanjanam (after all that haranguing, Perumal needs a bath!), and later in the evening a dhvadhasa thiruvaradhanam with twelve lamps. Finally, late in the evening, the Saptavarana Puranam Sevital–this refers to the seven square structural enclosures built one within the other around a temple's garba griham, the most famous example of which is the Sri Ranganathaswamy Temple in Srirangam. Perumal circles the prakaram seven times to bless all tiers of creation that these enclosures represent. Devotees gather during this time to sing traditional texts (like the Thiruppanimolai). Sapta (seven), Avaranam (enclosure or layer), Puranam (sacred history/tradition), and Sevital/Seva (worshipful visitation or service).
The day’s schedule:
8AM: Vimana purappadu, Nachiyar, samvadam, Mattaiadi Utsavam
11AM: Dwadasha Kalasa Thirumanjanam
7PM: Dwadasharadhanam, Chandra Prabhai Veethi purappadu
10PM: Saptavarana Puranam Sevital

notes.title: The Utsavam, Classifications, Changing Compulsions and Forms
body: Spoke to one of the temple Gurukkals about Damanotsava (Davanotsavam), but the name did not at all appear familiar to him, let alone the ritual. Instead he classed utsavas according to Siva’s 5 great cosmic acts, which we presume is in alliance with the Shiva Purana: Vidyesvara Samhita, Adhyaya 10, Shloka 2 given below:
सृष्टिः स्थितिश्च संहारस्तिरोभावोऽप्यनुग्रहः । पंचैव मे जगत्कृत्यं नित्यसिद्धमजाच्युतौ
sṛṣṭiḥ sthitiśca saṃhārastirobhāvo'pyanugrahaḥ | paṃcaiva me jagatkṛtyaṃ nityasiddhamajācyutau
Creation, preservation, dissolution, concealment, and grace—these five alone are My cosmic acts with regard to the universe; I, the Unborn and the Imperishable, accomplish them eternally.

Sṛṣṭi, Sthiti, Saṃhāra, Tirobhāva and Anugraha. The Gurukkal mapped each of these onto specific temples: Anugraha is Mayiladuthurai; Samhara is Thiruchendur and Mylapore-Kapaleeswara; Vedapuriswara is a Srishthi utsavam temple, which means that the more shanti-giving rites are less important. Not sure if this is his own interpretation or some wider understanding.

Later, he mentions Pacchai saathupadi /பச்சை சாத்துப்படி அலங்காரம் as a version of what he called damanotsavam – decorating with marikozhunthu and vettiver, for their calming and cooling effects. But this has no resonance with anything we’ve read so far about the Damanotsavam, which appears to be all but lost from local Saiva practice.

The Gurukkal spoke a lot about the idea of the bhaktostavam as the definite type of ritual at Vedapuriswara, because here (unlike Perumal koyil), difficulties are many, funds are scarce, and bhaktas and ubhayakaras are the driving forces because they sponsor. There is therefore the need to show the grandeur or effectiveness of an alankaram to convince them to take on the expense the next year. What comes to the priests for this is marginal, which is part of the reason they tend to seek employment abroad even for short periods. In the latest brahmotsavam many such things were done that were above and beyond what was paid – an excess by any other name – so that the ubhayakaras are convinced their money is being well used and will accept the higher charges next time (almost a freemium model, or a persuasive methodology).

Separating pujas and temple events into those which must remain fixed and those in which the rules can be bent. Fixed ones must continue and never diminish. “Utsavams” are fixed, “Bhaktotsavams” are flexible. Others can come and go by circumstance and capacity. But expectations are formative, generative, and the world beyond the temple creates these in no small measure. For example, Annadanam as a practice that is growing in importance–prasadam in the past was a mere spoonful, not more. But now the primary expectation is: darshanam, prasadam; sight and food, in quantity. Not given in the bare hand either (as sometimes the Perumal Koyil insists it should be): Elai-la potta-thaan prasadam, only if there’s enough to be put on a leaf, it’s prasadam. This feeds into the idea that we’re pressing temples to come up with foods as their distinguishing elements, which may be true of some Vaishnava kshetrams but not so much Saiva.

It’s worth consulting Davis here on the Mahotsavavidhi of Aghorasiva, Introduction pg 45: “The most unambiguous reference to devotional hymns in Mahotsavavidhi, however, comes in the “festival of the Devotees” (bhaktotsava), which takes place after the completion of the regular nine-day festival. In this ceremony, icons of the Devotees are honored and praised with devotional hymns, though Aghoras´iva does not specify what those hymns are. Further, “those who know the S´aiva songs” receive cloth and other special gifts at this festival event. It is likely that Aghoras´iva has in mind specialist singers of the Tamil S ´aiva hymns of the Tevaram.”
Also: [Davis: bhaktotsava (festival of the Devotees), 45, 61–62, 134–136 ]

He also spoke about the temple itself, and its Kodi maram or Dvajasthamba. It is clad with metal, inside is wood. There was an older kodi maram, mahotsavams would happen, but the wood disintegrates, and so they re-start the brahmotsavams only after reinstalling it. In 1946 there was a Kumbhabhishekam, after that the maram must have fallen and next Kumbhabhishekam happened in 1976 – only after which the current Mahotsavam tradition has started.

Siva’s simplicity appeals to him, as a ritualist. The “aadambarai” left for the outside, inside only what I truly am, simple and light alankaram. Which is also why the deity is relieved of all these weights He carries at night, to rest.

notes.title: Signalling the Start of a Temple Renovation
body: We hear of this by total coincidence, while in pursuit of Sridhar Gurukkal for a conversation. To our dismay (because otherwise the utsavams would have proceeded in full force), the Manakkula Vinayaka temple is preparing for its next Kumbabhishekam, and a Balayalam has been scheduled. Literally, this is the designation of a temporary, ritually consecrated place in which a temple deity's presence is maintained while the main shrine undergo renovation, repair or ritual renewal – Bala (child) + Aalaya (abode), Bālālaya is the temporary shrine; bālālaya-pratiṣṭhā or bālālaya-kumbhābhiṣekam refers to its ritual establishment.

Technically this is scheduled for July 5, but the preparatory pujas and first Kalam happen on July 4, starting with abhisekams in the morning and shanti pujas in the evening. We were there till around 830pm, caught the tail end of the Vastu shanti pujas, saw rakshai being tied for rakshai for several priests, several agni kundams set up, each with a requisite number of kalasas each, the main agni kunda with kalashas on all four as though marking an ellai or boundary, with a leaf with jaggery piece in front, 2 pictures each of the dashabhujas (Mooshika, conch, chattram, sword, and several others including a small male figure on the south west side).

4 priests were anointed, 1 for each of the murtis: Balavinayaka, Murugan, Chandiswara and the Moolavar. Pujas happened at each place, with 2 cords, one red like erukkam twine connecting the kalasas at the top of each vimanam with the thread-adorned kalasas below, each wound beautifully with colored strings. Pujas go on for each by separate priests, who then carry the kalasas to the main homam area. The puja for the main vimana is done by the main priest for this occasion (he’s from Kalahasti), sitting on the top of the vimana itself.
Dinamalar reports the following on July 5, 2026:
Puducherry: The Balalayam (preliminary consecration ritual) was held yesterday at the Puducherry Manakula Vinayagar Temple.

The last Kumbhabhishekam (grand consecration) at the Puducherry Manakula Vinayagar Temple was conducted in April 2015. As 12 years are about to pass since the previous ceremony, the temple management decided to perform the Kumbhabhishekam.

Following that decision, the preliminary Balalayam work for the Kumbhabhishekam commenced yesterday. During the ceremony that began at 10:30 AM, special Abhishekam (ritual bathing) and Aaradhana (worship) were performed for Lord Manakula Vinayagar. Governor Kailashnathan, MLA Vignesh Kannan, and other dignitaries attended the event.

The temple renovation and restoration work is planned to be completed within ten months. The temple management stated that during the days when the Kumbhabhishekam preparation works take place, all special prayers, Abhishekam, and Aaradhana for Lord Manakula Vinayagar will continue as usual. The arrangements were carried out by the temple priests (Sivacharyas) Ganesh, Nagaraj, and Seenu.

notes.title: Balalayam Homams Continue
body: Homam going on as I (Arun) walk in. Kalahasti priest was in front of the big kumbham again. Goes on for about half an hour. Then deeparadhanai for the main kumbham, very well done. All five kumbham/kalasas are carried by the respective priests for one ul-purappadu. The governor and an mla are there, so everybody seems to flock towards them and not the kalasas. After ul-purappadu, kalasas all go into utsava mandapa and are placed there to remain until the end of thirumeni. One last deeparadhanai from there, and balalayam concludes.
I try to reach out to the kalahasti priest. Complimented him on how beautifully he did all the mudras. He walks on before I can ask for contact details.

notes.occasion: Searching for Damana at Goubert Market
body: We went to Draupadi Amman for their Adi masam vizha patrikai, Kamakshi amman to clarify Aadi masam pujas (found a new young cockerel there), Mutthumariamman to get Jnanavel Swamy’s number, Ellaiamman to get Santosh Gurukkal’s number.

Went to market for Panneer elai, found Masi Pachai (மாசி பச்சை), only [scientifically known as Artemisia vulgaris (commonly called Mugwort or Common Wormwood], Davanam, Maruvam and வெட்சிப் பூ / idli poo/ Ixora. We also got photos of the statues strewn around – bits that had presumably been part of the Genji/Senji temple ruins, brought to Pondicherry as “decor” in French times, much like the tall pillars that once surrounded the Dupleix statue and now thankfully circle Gandhi thatha on the beach–with one stray one in fact placed close to the clock tower in the market. There’s a Vishnudurga and a Bhairava (hidden by a tomato vendor), two Lingodbhava statues, and some others.

The plaza in the center is the market’s bell tower or periya mani gundu, given to the city by one Diagou Moudaliar (Thiyagu Moudaliar), a descendent of Lazaro de Motta Tanappa Moudaliar, who became the first Dubash of Pondicherry in 1674. He became Christian, presumably to further his own fortunes, and was appointed the chief agent of the French East India Company. He was instrumental in facilitating the arrival of French officials and native migrants in Pondicherry in January 1674. In 1686, he was appointed the head of the Tamil merchants, gaining full authority over the company's commercial transactions with local merchants, fixing prices, and establishing textile production and storage hubs in Pondicherry. His son, Andre Muthappa Mudaliar, subsequently assumed commercial responsibilities as dubash starting around 1699, followed later by his grandson, Pedro Kanakaraya Mudaliar, who also served as Chief Dubash. These are names you will see around and on street signs in the older Christianized parts of Pondicherry town, where now old remnants of Hindu temples are treated as decor. It is in the center of what is now “Goubert market” or Pondicherry’s central wet market. The belfry was built by the engineer Louis Guerre.

(The market is larger than the Chinna Kadai market with its Petite clock tower. The periya mani gundu was built in 1851 and is still called the Diagou Mudaliar Clock Tower. It was placed there in order to beautify the black town's fountain, which brought Mutrapalayam water to Pondicherry town).

To its north-western corner, the market also holds a little shrine to Vinayaka – the Varasiddhi Veeravinayaka Thirukkoyil. The priest is there at 11, presumably for the uccikala puja, and offers lemon-rice prasadam for those around. The narrow prakaram houses two stone inscriptions, the undated older one announcing a “noothana thiruppani” and the newer 2012 one announcing the last the Kumbhabhishekam.
Notes from all over, here synthesized.

notes.title: The First Time We Were Called to Thiruvahindrapuram, We Didn’t Go
body: Went to Perumal koyil – had a quick chat with Ramanan Bhattacharya about damana utsavam – He says it happens in a few Perumal temples, including Kanchi. Mostly in Masi, but here they do on Chithirai pournami as that’s otherwise a “low” month. Not a maasam utsavam though. Can be done any month when damana is plentiful, and that’s Masi /Panguni /Chithirai. No burning of damana, no question of it. But he seemed less interested in our questions than in re-directing us to Thiruvahindrapuram. There they do a Danavanthiri alankaram, he said: they take all the mooligai and make powder and distribute as prasadam. If we leave by 3 get back to Pondy by 4, then we can come to Perumal for Ramar ul-purappadu, because it’s Punarpoosam, his birth nakshatram.

It was our loss not to heed his directions, as we would later find when we went there for the Ratnangi Sevai during the Desikar Utsavam. We reached the Perumal Koyil for the purappadu late, too, and the Bhattacharya remarked on that.

notes.title: Chandana-Chandana-Chandana!
body: Chandana kaappu for Angalamman that made her look like a little bommai (doll). The gurukkal later sent us photos, which you can see. At Mutthumariamman, too, chandana kaappu.

At the Iswaran Koyil, too, chandana kaappu, but done in green (no photos here) so it did not look like chandanam but like a garment. I asked Arasoo Swamy who had done the alankaram, and he replied “when you ask like that, we will always say that we did it.” One of many lessons for me in the deflection of self and ego that happens in the temples. There is no “I” as such (thaan-gara ahambhavam, my Amma used to say), there is perhaps a collective “we” and the certainly of a HIM or a HER.

A little like the Ghousiga temple has its Thulasi Mariamman, the Lawspet Murugan Koyil has a Balamutthumariamman koyil about a block away, and considers both shrines “one.” Balamutthumariamman should have had a vizha starting today, but we only heard of it and weren’t around to see for ourselves.

notes.title: The Great Festival of Draupadi Starts Modestly
body: Very small puja. Not more than a dozen in attendance, including us. Abhishekam is just milk and water – we arrive midway. No elaborate rituals, all conducted by priest and the teacher whom we’ve met at the temple, who serves as his assistant. No adambaram for me, says the priest – and the simple alankarams reinforce this. We’re given malas and fruits etc – like ubhayakaras! It’s “our festival" thanks to the small contribution made for this event.
Day 0 or: Vināyakar Pūjā (Worship of Gaṇeśa) Śrī Vedavyāsar & Group,No. 136, Kāmarāj Amman Temple Street, Puducherry.

Also went to Lalit’s garden to see Vadivelou Sir dance. The program started unforgivably late, so we only caught the first item (Bhavayami Gopala Balam) at 730pm before we had to leave for the temple.

notes.title: Draupadi Amman’s Bright Yellow Flag Raising
body: The temple calls 2 Iyers for this event and the Thirukalyanam, and does all other days’ rituals independently. The two Iyers present have been associated with this Vanniar community and this event for a long time, it’s a mutually supportive relationship. The Arohanam as such, as a result, follows a familiar pattern. Draupadi Amman is out with Perumal and Arjuna, wooden and brass forms of Pothuraja out in front, the flag cloth is simple yellow-dyed, and a mud pot is prepared like a kalasham with threads.

The priest carries the pot, and then he and a small group walk to and into Vedapuriswara via the south entrance, and go straight to the Kulam. The Amman’s trident strung with jasmine precedes them, as does the wooden form of Pothuraja, leading the way with the Nadaswaram player Venkat and the tavil. They placed the kalasham just at the entrance of the kulam. The priest goes to the water to bathe, with two others who help him. He wears a new yellow garment (dhoti, but tied at knee length like a pair of shorts), his body is strung with jasmine malas making an X across his chest and back, and his arms anointed with the Vaishanava namam. Then they collect water from the kulam as theertham in the one mud pot. They do an aradhanai for the pot right there, and walk out of the temple by going around the main shrine and out the front entrance, rounding the corner, and back onto the Iswaran Dharmaraja Koyil street.

When they come back to the temple, it’s one pradakshina round here, too, their feet are washed by the dwajasthamba, anointed with turmeric and kunkuma, and the pot with the theertham goes into the garba griha which is now all clad in brass. It comes out to the homam area shortly, and sits with the other kalashas there. The priest and Prakash (who will carry the Karagam) wear poonals (which are placed on the bodies of the waiting deities as well), the homam commences. There are a whole lot of kaappu around, with turmeric pieces pre-tied. These go around all who are participants in the Vizha, wrists of human hands, the bodies of statues like that of Pothuraja, around the dwajasthamba itself. Poornahuti happens, the flag is anointed with mango leaves, a jasmine mala, and darba grass, and carried around the temple prakaram. Priest carries the earthenware kalasham, Prakash has the flag itself. But at some point they switch, because it’s Rangaradjou swamy who actually hoists the flag. Once the ceremony is done, the theertha kalasham goes back into the garba griha, and it’s time for the evening’s purappadu!

notes.title: The Yellowest Dravyam of Them All
body: 3pm on the 1st Tuesday of Aadi Masam is a Manja neer/Kuzhambu Abhishekam at the Kamakshi Amman temple. The dravyangal or substances used in all the thousand abhishekams happening in this town need better reflection and treatment than we can offer here, so for now just the process. One lady from Kannika who is here also instructs us to buy “gopura manjal” from the shop next door. We do. It’s given to a man who is preparing the kuzhambu by vigorously mixing all the received turmeric with water – turmeric isn’t water soluble, so this produces at best a thick suspension (a point which becomes relevant later, as you’ll see). Too much liquid, and the suspension won’t feel like a kuzhambu at all. “Kuzhambu” because of its kozhai-kozhai “slippery-thick” texture. Then the Iyer comes over and chides the group for using water instead of paneer or rose water for fragrance. So, two bottles of rose water go in. Now the kuzhambu isn’t so kozha-kozha, so more turmeric goes in. It’s plentiful anyway, with many bringing packets in.

This whole gundaan was carried into the garba griha, where the abhishekam began. Visibility here was a little challenging, so I positioned myself outside, by the pranala, where the yellow liquid was eminently visible and strikingly so against the temple walls’ light blue. A group of men soon came over with a red cloth and a patram to catch the falling turmeric. Once it had flown over the deity’s body, it was sacred of course. It took several men and many more than several minutes for the liquid all to be collected, with the red cloth serving as strainer. The same hands that had worked to mix the turmeric now worked again to allow the water to flow out of it. Many women and others hung out by the pranala with us, catching the water in their own bottles and commenting on how they just needed to have it settle to collect the sacred turmeric.

The men then carried the “bag” of turmeric indoors, where they spread it out and started fashioning it into balls. Women soon took over – the scene went from being all men to being all women. The turmeric “laddoos” were laid out on trays near the sannadhi to rest or perhaps dry slightly. The Iyer came out with chandanam for everyone, the colour of which was virtually indistinguishable from the turmeric (a sign of adulteration, in that case, as chandanam should properly be just beige or brown).
There was another group of women making malas for the Goddess. We watched them work for a while. A kunkumarchana and sahasranama recital followed, after which there was the customary deeparadhanai.

It may be sacrilege to ask why this abhishekam couldn’t have been done with plain dry turmeric, the way vibhuti is used sometimes for Murugan and Siva. But the point is never just convenience or efficiency; in fact in so many of these rituals it’s an explicit setting aside of personal convenience that is considered proper, valuable, necessary.
