EVENING: Mutthupallakku came from Perumal, a massively long caterpillar like thing. Manikarar told me to pay attention to it turning corners and how it flexes there but it did not seem to have any particular character there at all. The drummer team was good but the sounds never came together and beyond a point, along with pataas and all, it was just noise. Amman in the garba griha was Kamakshi (both feet folded, had one been hanging she’d have been Raja Rajeshwari; they put a kili in one hand but normally there’d have been a flower one of the pusaris told me). Utsavar was Mariamman herself, in full form. Jnanavel Swamy was very pleased. It was 9 by the time the procession started (pallakku stopped at the head of the street, utsavar was carried out to meet it), and it seemed to hang for long in front of the temple. So we left around 9 or thereafter.

Spent some time talking to an elderly lady called Saroja of one of the stone inscriptions, whose name is Tamil Arasi or just Tamil. Distinguished looking lady. She said her mother had been the one to build the older gopuram, and then she + others did a layer each of the present one at the last Kumabhishekam. But the older inscription is gone–temples appear not good at all about keeping their histories in this way. Clearly this made her feel sad. Spoke a bit about how there had been problems in the temple admin. before and so she and some others had been brought in as the nirvagam. Govt. officer appointed 1980. But who knows what they do?

notes.title: All These Ways to Call to Vinayaka
body: Single woman ubhayam (the same lady who comes daily to do the Lalita Trishati archanai). Kalyana gurukkal and the other priest whom we’ve seen before doing the puja. Hardly anyone present at first, some doing circumabulations needing to be told not to cross the puja area. Slowly a group gathers, but it’s never very big.
At the Chetty koyil, the crowd is bigger but the proceedings are not much different. Modakams are given as offerings to Agni! The priest who does the Durga abhishekam for them is officiating.
A bit later in the afternoon, Nandhikeswara priests are at the Gangai Vinayaka temple, which is of course the Vinayaka shrine that pre-dates and was open long before the Nandhikeshwara.
The schedule here: Sri Gangai Vinayagar Maha Sankatahara Chaturthi: (31/08, Monday)

list: 4:30 PM - 5:30 PM – Sakala Abhishekam, 108 Sanghabhishekam (Conch Abhishekam)

body: And as ever with this temple, the aesthetics are just absolutely perfect. We’ve by now seen so many Shankhabhishekams, but none where the conches are laid out this beautifully, in almost a perfect grid. They were laid out by the well, and the afternoon light streams in from behind there, so perhaps that had an effect as well. The agni kundam was just in front of the conches, and the priests sat on the N-S ends. They had books open and were reading Tamil script as all the pujas here are done in Tamil, but we forgot to ask them what specifically the recitations are. After the poornahuti, the shankhabhishekam begins–and here, too, is a beautiful process because each conch is picked up and very carefully passed on, person-to-person, all the way to the garba griha where it is poured on the waiting Vinayaka. Everyone there takes the task very seriously. While I understand entirely why the priests at other temples keep the ritual objects in their care alone, there is something very relieving about Nandhikeswara’s participatory processes overall.

The abhishekam itself is being videographed by a media man of unfortunately wide width, so we can barely see what is going on. Alankaram takes very, very long though each time the time-estimation is “half an hour” so we rely on the photograph sent out by the Dewan later for the final chandana-kaappu look!

Back at the Chetty Koyil in the evening is an Unjal utsavam. We reached just before 7 when the utsavar + siddhi buddhi was being taken to the unjal. Some kerfuffle getting it onto the cart for the pradakshina. Took some time to get the unjal set up. Dance was about to happen but we left.
Is this also the Chetty Koyil Aandu Vizha? A poster to that effect is on file.

notes.title: A Quick Stop and a Not-So-Quick Chat
body: Utsava murti abhishekam earlier in the morning. Crowd at Balavinayaka.

Spoke for some time to a Gurukkal we know there about the growing impatience of the temple-going crowds with long rituals that are in fact more important than some of the others most often seen. For example, the Panchasana puja is supposed to be done along with kaalam pujai. Is it being done? It will take ½ hour, with the screen closed. Who wants this? Deeparadhanai and Alankara is what constitute “puja”--another instance of a movement in a devotee-centric directions that displace the full array of agamic/tantric ritual practices.

What changes will this thiruppani bring? During a prior kumabhishekam, they broke the wall separating the temple from the current mandapam area. Per agamas, temples should have a closed inner prakaram (as it is in Perumal koyil); the circulation of devotees in this prakaram is part of what gives the power to the deity. But here that’s gone for the sake of a free open environment and convenience.

He spoke also about Sanskrit and Tamil, so often pitted and in tension if you read the newspapers or listen to all those Periyar pethis out there: to see “mudra roopam” you need Sanskrit, but to rouse emotions there’s no language other than Tamil. He spoke for the place of each, placing emphasis on the former for visualising and on the latter for connecting. We thought it an interesting, integrative, and balanced perspective.

notes.title: Thanga Ther Ul-Purappadu
body: Lawspet Murugan Koyil puja begins with Vinayaka (pattern: Venkatesan gurukkal chants, then 2 others sing thiruppugazh in Tamil, there is a small aradhanai – this is repeated grandly in the main sannathi, where there’s the full deeparadhanai, then the priest goes around all the other shrines while people follow, ending up at the utsavar where the full puja happens again including all lamps. Nadaswaram and Thavil throughout. Then someone brings the thanga ther, the utsavar is brought on and 3 of the ubhayakaras are turbaned [with the silk parivattam] [Shesha-vastra honour (Parivattam, பரிவட்டம்)] and they pull it once in the prakaram. Followed by another puja and the utsavars are returned to starting position (but still in the ther) while all the ubhayakaras present are given madaryada. The ther itself is a bit too gold and lit up but this feels right for this community’s expression of its aspirations and aesthetic sense. The point is more that this is done to their taste and according to their means, it’s neither too grand nor unnoticeable. And no compromise on the pujas, which are well done and feel complete. There’s a crowd but a quiet one, not unbearable, pushing etc.

[*the parivattam is connected with the head being prepared to receive something belonging to the Lord. The person receiving the honour is being marked as one occupying a position of reverence before the Lord.]

Murugan utsavar has a very simple alankaram. Satrified with gold, and one white malli garland. The upachara rite is done very beautifully – the vilakkus are clean, are organised neatly on a specific stand before and after their use, and they are presented to Murugan in a fairly well-choreographed manner. It is simple, but done with deliberation and presence of mind, and that gives it its beauty.
Not sure how to compare this to Vedapuriswara or Nandikeswara. Each of the three temples are as though in leagues of their own.

notes.title: Pandarinatha and Krishna Utsavar Thirumanjanam
body: The Pandarinatha Thirumanjanam happens in honor of His nakshatra naal, which is Rohini nakshatram.

At 930pm (supposed to be)/ 1045pm (when it actually begins) there was a Perumal, Venugopalan, Navaneethakrishnan and baby Thavazhum Kannan Thirumanjanam. Finishes by 1145. We leave by midnight as the rest wait on for the moon to grow visible as it is only then that the puja will be completed.

Observation made by the Draupadi Amman temple priest at a different moment but relevant here: Gokulashtami and Krishna Jayanti fall this year on the same date. So that means that some years they fall on different dates? How? The explanation is that people observe the moment differently. Most observe the ‘thithi’ – the ashtami (eighth day of the month) of the month Shravan/Aavani, in which case it is by its very name associated with the thithi, Gokulashtami or Janmashtami. But there are others who observe the Aavani birth star which is Rohini, and they call it Krishna Jayanti (or Sri Jayanti).

notes.title: Bhairava Abhishekam
body: In the morning, there was an abhishekam done for Bhairavar, sponsored by the lady who seems to carry so much at this temple – the trishati archana, the Sankatahara chaturthi homam, the Navaratri gopujas. But this was not the theipirai ashtami abhishekam! This happens in the evening around 6pm.

notes.title: A Temple Grows from a Temple
body: There is a Krishna shrine just outside the Sundara VInayaka temple, which turns out not to be the temple’s own at all. A neighborhood group used to rent a statue and do their Jayanti pujas, but over time this became a proper physical shrine which shares physical space (the position of the shrine itself, the use of the road outside, the use of the temple space itself for alankaram) – and I’m not sure whether to read this as compulsion or cooperation. During Jayanti, they are doing a Sudarshana homam, Krishna Abhishekam was supposed to start 1030, but hadn’t begun by noon. We took a few representative photos and frankly putting it sneaked out. We didn’t want to appear to support a temple that was a bit at odds with the family’s temple which we were following for this project.

The priest performing Homam was from Chetty Koyil, also the helper and the nadaswaram-thavil players. How can sivacharyas perform sudarshana homas? We ask him. Vaishnava priests only for Perumal, but Krishna was Yadava so anyone can do, was the reply.

In the evening, we came again, to see some kids there dressed as Krishnas as there are many yadavas in the neighborhood; alankaram for the Krishna being done (to make him look like he’s eating butter). Actually, we came to try to see the 4pm Kalabhairava abhishekam – but hadn’t started by 5, Rani ma’am calls me at 6, but I’m unable to go then. They’re having trouble keeping up with the demands of the temple and are in search of a priest to do regular nityapadi pujas. Her atthai installed the Murugan idol, and does a Murugan Thirukalyanam during Sashti every year. They hold it in the hall they have upstairs from the main temple.

notes.title: Chetty Perumal’s Two Point Uriyadi Utsavam
body: Uriyadi Utsavam only at two points. First South gate, then North gate. We catch them briefly as they complete the uriyadi on the Southern street. Unlike Perumal Koyil which begins uriyadi on the Southern road, Chetty ends on the Southern road because the Perumal comes out of the North and completes the uriyadi there first. We notice the splashes on the Northern road as we pass by a little later.

உரியடி உற்சவம் – the words are உரி and அடி – the strung-together pots used to keep butter and curd out of the hands of mischievous, hungry children (and “foraging” animals), which are then beaten (adi!) with a long stick while the task is made more complicated by the showering of water by “screeners” on the sides. A decorated triangular “flag” that’s meant to stand in for an earthenware pot (filled with curd, turmeric water, milk, or sweets/coins) along with murukus, athirasam and other treats strung alongside is suspended high above the ground using a rope-and-pulley setup. A man controls this, making it go up-down, while young folks hit with a long stick to try to get the prize. The imaginary pot is of course venerated as an extension of Perumal, whose utsavars stand and watch the show. Likewise, the young men participating in the Uri-Adi are in yellow veshtis, with just banians or bare-chested. A gamefied sevai, perhaps!

notes.title: Perumal’s Four Point Uriyadi Utsavam
body: 8am - Venugopalan and Navaneethakrishnan come out of the shadows of the Ramar Sannathi for their single annual appearance. One would expect this one-off emergence to be a great crowd-puller, but the temple is surprisingly empty. Perhaps the keenest of devotees had their fill past midnight last night, when all the Krishnas had an aradhanai under the moonlit sky. The two Krishnas are exquisite in their yellow-red adornments and their emergence is splendid. Albeit only an ul-purappadu, watching Navaneethakrishnan joyfully dance butter-in-hand on the morning of the uriyadi utsavam was very sweet.

After 630pm - the uriyadi utsavam’s purappadu began. It was Perumal – in the form of Krishna climbing up a ladder towards a butter-pot – who came out. Once on the street, He stopped along the southern madaveethi to allow for dances followed by the uriyadi. We can’t tell if the dances with the sticks are South Indian or Garba-Dandiya inspired. The Gopis nonetheless had the effect of urging Krishna to reach and smash the butter-pot. The uri itself was merely decorative paper or plastic, with tiny pots hanging at the bottom. Once the boys stepped up with their sticks, it was all drama and excitement. The uri hanging from a pulley was pulled and controlled by a gentleman who kept it teasingly out of the boys’ sticks’ reach. To add to the stimulation, bucket after bucket of water was splashed on the boys’ faces as they reached out to smack the uri. After a significant back-and-forth, the uri was finally hit and caught, concluding the first of the uriyadis of the night. By the looks of it, the same uri will be tied at the different points – madaveethi south (what we saw), madaveethi north, and on the two northern and southern crossings of Mission Street.

notes.title: Brahmanda Set Up for Periyandavar
body: This was actually a private tonsuring and ear piercing ceremony done on temple premises, as a ritual activity for those who see Periyandavar as their kula deivam. Jnanavel Swami invited us to be there, for “coverage” and to spread awareness about these sorts of pujas. He’s also walked us through the stone inscriptions at the back of the temple – his own name appears on several occasions. Deekay enterprises is another big donor – they’re an import-export company, Jnanavel Swami tells us.

The pusari who is hard of hearing is the “specialist” called in specifically to create the periyandavar temple-in-temple. He uses semmannu to fashion all the deities; they are just semi-conical structures with a flat base on which to stand. Lingam, by any other form. Kolam lines mark out where they stand and delineate the sacred area as a whole. It is a devar sabhai. Outside this delineation, facing the devar sabhai is Muthalarajan – alcohol consuming, bread-eating, meat-eating Muthalarajan [though it remains to be verified who it is]. Outside to the right is Puttru/Poothamman – and she’s made in the anthill form, too, in accordance with her name, and is eventually dressed in a sari and decorated with neem and jasmine. To the left is a figure who must be Vinayaka, though a man we meet (a photographer, curious about our orientations and work) tells us that that place was occupied once by a rural/folk being or divinity that has now merged and become associated with Ganapati. He didn’t sound dravidianist or dismissive of the popular Hindu pantheon, and this makes me think again about associations and how such associative practices have materialized insights that may indeed have once been subtle thoughts and ideas expressed tenuously, and slowly in this fashion consolidated.

Within the devar sabhai is Kathavarayan, whom Muthalarajan must face. At his four corners are four boundary or direction-guarding figures. At the far back, protected by Kathavarayan, is Periyandavar – Sivaperuman – flanked by Iccha Shakti and Kriya Shakti (Jnanavel Swami said), or by Brahma and Vishnu (the trimurti) if you follow other interpretations of the sabhai set-up. The outer frame of the space is held by a series of smaller figures, arranged in clusters of varied even and uneven numbers. They are the nayanars, Jnanavel told us, or other deified, revered beings holding the space together. In some rural areas, the idea is to have 108 pillayars around (Ara puja = 54; Kaal puja = 27), each one getting a padayal (with 108 broken coconuts) and a maa-vilakku (the maa-vilakku is essential, and several were made for this puja, too). Or other gatherings are: Ashtadigbalargal (for 8 directions), 7 rishi-gal, 5 Lingams - pancha bhootam, 4 Vedas, and 9 Grahas. The number 108 is important.
[Is there a Saraswati-Varalakshmi-Ambikai trio also?]

Why is everyone invoked though? Why not only Periyandavar? – Because when you call someone for a function, you don’t just call them, you call the whole family. Traditionally in villages, the ubhayakara collects bhiksha – rice, dal etc. – as a beggar. The puja is performed to unite the village, and to make Periyandavar the town’s deivam, the world’s Lord.

Rice flour slurry is poured upon each form, followed by turmeric slurry. Chandanam splashed on and not poured presumably owing to cost. This is the equivalent of an abhishekam, though it is an adding of auspicious substances, not a removing of impurities. Then each figure gets kunkumam pottus: three vertically downwards for lesser forms, and the tripundra also in kumkumam. Kola maavu lines are replicated with yellow thread that now marks, an inch or two above ground, the form of the whole temple [also called kautuka (कौतुक)]. In the center where Kathavarayan stands, it’s made to criss-cross in a form that resembles a mandala.

Small neem sticks inserted into the still-soft mud of the deities’ forms become makeshift stands to support the flower malas. Banana leaves are placed in front, vettrilai, banana, and a semblance of a meal: curd-rice with a touch of panchamritam poured on top. Neem leaves. Arali malas. Jasmine.

The whole set-up takes hours, and the puja itself merely minutes. Is it ok that the ritual element of Amman temple worship takes so little time? A Gurukkal we met later told us that the communities who run these temples are non-vegetarians, and only they can sustain the forces that are called upon in such shrines – so it is perfectly alright for their ritual processes to be different from the mainstream Saiva temples.

Karpooram is placed in front of each form to invoke Siva’s agni-roopam. In the villages there would have also been bali, animal sacrifice – a chicken, a goat, a pig. But in town that practice has long since been discontinued.

Traditional ear piercing happens after it all, much to the little guy’s great distress. And the phone held out showing cartoons was not helping. The puja as such was very short – camphor lit, Vinayaka propitiated, then Periyandavar at the back (at whose feet was placed a piece of the tonsured hair, with jasmine).

Their unique Kubera yantra archanai happens on Thursdays and has been very elusive for us. Even today we are unable to go for it. The Kuberan Yantra was apparently present on the building site when the temple was constructed in 1921, and identified as such by Kanchi Periyavar (or someone allied). A fitting presence for a community of merchants, many in the precious metals and fabrics trade! An Abhishekam to the Yantra happens monthly once on Poosa nakshatram. Archanais are a weekly affair.

notes.title: Telugu Observances in Tamil Country
body: We found from their whiteboard yesterday: Sarva Amaavaasai (Polaala Amaavaasai), but we could not go for it.

Polala Amavasya (also known as Polamba Vratham or Shravana Amavasya) is a traditional Hindu festival observed on the new moon day (Amavasya) of the Shravana month in the Telugu calendar; Dedicated to Goddess Poleramma (or Pochamma).

notes.title: A Little Big Day?
body: Big day for Sundara Vinayaka as their Brahmotsavam begins – one would think. But perhaps not, given the air of laidbackness that permeates. The time given on patrikai: 6am to 9am. I get there at 630am to find the temple still locked from the previous night. It takes me three back and forth trips over the next 2 hours to finally catch them – not beginning the puja – but beginning to prepare for the puja. At 9am. That’s a three-hour delay. Yikes. At 9am the priests begin to settle in, tying thread around the kalasas and pulling out packets of manjal, kumkumam, etc from their bags. The two utsava murtis of Vinayaka are taken into the garbhagrham. This preparation goes on for two hours, while some odhuvars and assistant priests trickle in. Finally, at 11am, five hours after the scheduled time, the homam begins. The abhishekam inside also happens simultaneously, saving a handful of minutes after the 5 hour delay – “the economical Indian”, I thought to myself.

As the homam and abhishekam are completed, kalasas are carried by Rani madam and her husband for three rounds of ul-purappdu. Kalasa abhishekam is done inside, and the flag is raised. This happens rather unceremoniously, with one bell tinkling, and nobody really paying much attention. The moola Vinayakar and his two utsavars are seated without any alankaram after their abhishekam. Once the flag is raised, everybody waits for the alankaram which is done by a rather young priest-boy, maybe 13 or 14 years of age. Once done, he is praised for it by an older priest who assisted in the homam. This is followed by deeparadhanai and prasadam. The ul-purappadu was to happen after everybody was done with prasadam, and it’s already 1230, so I took my leave.

A local artist has been called in to draw a photographic kolam of Balavinayaka. Nine Vinayakas get abhishekam here: Karpaga Vinayakar, Vaayir Vinayaka, Siva Vinayaka, Shakti Vinayakar, Polla Vinayakar (who is said to have revealed the tevaram manuscripts to Nambi), Narttana Vinayakar (koshta), Somaskanda Vinayakar, Bala Ganapati (outer prakaram, back), Kashi Viswanathar Vinayakar, Siddhi-Buddhi Vinayakar.

The evening procession begins just as we get there. One ul-purappadu then out and away. Perhaps the most beautiful Vinayaka procession alankaram of the day. The colours are bright and vibrant, but not extravagant and flashy. They’re as though subdued, yet rich and deep. His proportions are very well balanced. And adding another layer of charm and puzzling curiosity is the elephant vahana on which this elephant-headed-one is carried!

notes.title: Nine Bathing Vinayakas
notes.occasion: Vinayaka Chaturthi, Abhishekam for All Vinayakars and Ul-Purappadu
body: Nine Vinayakas of the temple got a full abhishekam, with singing and chanting. The nine are: one outside and to the left of the gopuram, two inside, on either side of the gopuram, Narttana Vinayaka below the mahabalipeetham, another Narttana Vinayaka on the Southern Koshtha, Polla Pillaiyar with the Nayanars, Bhaktapuriswara shrine’s Vinayaka Sthalavrishka Vinayaka, Adigu Vinayaka (the moolavar), and the Vinayaka utsavar. We stayed only for the first 4 abhishekams, which alone took an hour or more.
We noticed that the Nayanars were all unclothed, presumably to get new vastrams today.

The young priest doing the abhishekams is thorough with it, not rushing through any of the substances. We leave as the abhishekam for the Narttana Ganapati on the southern koshtha begins – it is perhaps the first and only time we watch an abhishekam take place there.
The evening procession begins at 9pm as we reach there after Chetty. A simpler, smaller alankaram, with Vinayaka alone. He looks rather slim. We notice a little Nataraja pendant on his chest.

notes.title: The One Chaturthi to Rule Them All
body: We did not go because of excessive crowds and photo-taking restrictions. But this is their event schedule from the patrikai:

“On the upcoming Monday, 14.09.2026, on the occasion of the Sri Vinayagar Chaturthi festival, the temple doors will open at 4:00 AM in the early morning. On behalf of the temple administration, special Abhishekam (ritual bathing), Dhoopa Deepa (incense and lamp offering), Neivethiyam (food offering), and Deeparadhanai (worship with lit lamps) will be performed for Sri Manakkula Vinayagar. After performing the Deeparadhanai (light offering ritual), "Moolavar Sri Manakkula Vinayagar" will bless devotees adorned in a gold armor (Thanga Kavasam).”
Livestream (Thanthi TV) of the entire event on Britain Tamil Bhakti
We could not go, but this is the information from their notice board:

“Abhishekam Kaalai 9.30 Manikku Sri Mulaver Karpaka Vinayagar, Sri Vayirathu Vinayagar, Sri Shiva Vinayagar, Sri Sakthi Vinayagar, Sri Pollapillaiyar, Sri Nrithana Vinayagar, Sri Somaskantha Vinayagar, Sri Balaganapathi, Kasi Viswanathar Vinayagar, Matrum Sri Sithi Budhi Vinayagar Udan Deeparadhanai”
How does Angalamman have 10 Vinayakas?! We can think of just two from all of our visits during all these months!
“Iravu 7.00 Manikku Sri Sithi Budhi Sametha Vinayagar Veedhi Purappadu
Ubayathaarar: Namasivayam Chettiyar Pandu Devasthanam”

notes.occasion: Vinayaka Chaturthi, Gangai Vinayakar Thirumanjanam, Alankaram and Veethi Ula
body: 6am Thirumanjanam 9am in special decorations [சிறப்பு அலங்காரத்தில்]6:30 pm street procession [வீதி உலா உற்சவமும்]

We walked into the Gangai Vinayaka Temple just as the puja was going on. Vinayaka inside was in chandana kaappu, right leg crossing over his left, with an arm resting on it. He also has an erukkam malai hanging at his base.

In the evening also we reached there just as the utsavamurti alankaram was about to be offered puja. The alankaram was beautifully done with a lively selection of colours, although Vinayaka’s body seemed a little long for his proportions – something we hardly see with Nandhikeswara priests’ alankarams.
There was a rather precarious loading moment! but all went well.

Abhishekam was at 9am, and we reached only after it was done. Alankaram being done by a local pusari. He was also doing the alangaram – a simple one – for the utsavar, a Vamamukhi or Idampuri Vinayaka to mirror the form of the main murti. Got good pictures of the beautiful bronze. The form of an elephant pervades all of Vinayaka, not just his head. Noticed that other than the pot-belly and stout arms and fingers, his legs are also very elephantine, thick like tree trunks, supported by broad sturdy feet. Alangaram done for moola and the two utsavars - and we saw the aradhanai. It was rather deserted, with Rani madam herself not present. There was cooking to be done at home, so we left. The ul-purappadu should have happened soon after then.

notes.occasion: Shukla Panchami Perumal-Thayar Thirukalyanam, Desikar Utsavam Day 3
body: Aavani Shukla Panchami is the fixed tithi for Perumal and Thayar’s annual divine marriage. We go around 930am to check the state of affairs. We were puzzled to find a Desikar aradhanai going on as we came in. We were entirely unaware of the Desikar utsavam having begun already. We hear that it apparently began on Sunday the 13th. We are also startled by the large stage built on the Southern prakaram for the Thirukalyanam. The startle was largely because when the patrikai mentioned thirumanjanam for Perumal and Thayar, we assumed it would be two separate thirumanjanams for the two moola murtis, and consequently had not brought our cameras along. Instead we found this large stage, with the Perumal and Thayar utsava murtis being prepared for the anointment. Of course! How did that not come to our minds? We rushed to fetch our cameras.

Upon returning, as we waited for the thirumanjanam to begin, we were briskly called for help. Tagging along behind the man who reached out to us, we soon found ourselves sitting outside the Pandarinathar shrine, knotting manjal (yellow) threads which will be distributed after the kalyanam. Fair to say that we gladly allowed ourselves to be ‘roped’ into the work, and become ‘threads’ in the organic fabric of the temple’s functioning.

It is only around 11am that the Thirumanjanam begins. It is very extensive – the substances never end! Milk especially simply kept flowing, and the assortment of fruits came down on the deities like an avalanche.

PM – events extend up to midnight. Perumal and Thayar play flower-toss, exchange garlands, are fed bananas and milk, and head over to the mandapam. Ramanan Bhattacharya performs the homam. New clothes are presented to the Bride and Groom. Naresh Bhattacharya as Perumal, and Dinesh Bhattacharya as Thayar, partake in the homam and walk seven times around the sacred fire. After the thread-tying rites [mangalyam] are complete, Perumal-Thayar take an amorous stroll to the kulam, where the wedding chalices are poured out [what rite is this?], with the lovely accompaniment of Nadaswaram. Finally, dancing, they make their way into the kannadi palliyarai where they’re placed on an unjal, fed an assortment of fruits, before being allowed to retire for the night. It is 1230am when the divine marriage concludes.

Desikar sevai and purappadu in the evening. There are 7 adhyapakas singing, while Krishna Yajurveda parayanam goes on outside Andal sannathi. Purappadu begins around 730pm. Desikar comes outside the ardhamandapam, facing and awaiting Perumal’s blessings. Thathacharya loudly announces the coming of Perumal, and Perumal's Sadari comes out to bless Desikar.

Desikar goes on three ul-purappadus after, stopping at all corners every time, and once in front of the mirror on the first round. There are no interactions with any other shrines. No blessings to be got from or given to the alvars, Anjaneyar or Manavala Mamunigal. Shekhar Mama says that that happens only for Perumal or Thayar’s purappadus. So when they stop like so, is it Perumal receiving or giving blessings? At the end of the third round, outside his shrine, Desikar is offered aradhanai with a kumbham, presented food, and made to dance before returning to his shrine. This is followed by some more singing for the saattrumurai marking the end.

Hayagriva Koyil Venkatesa Bhattacharya’s wife tells me: Perumal’s nakshatram is hasta. Revathy for Ranganatha. Thiruvonam for others. She also talks about the composition of the Paduka Sahasram following a competition.

Krishna Yajurveda Parayanam: the one man who asks me to take video is from here, but the others have come from Chennai for this. Krishna Yajurveda, samhita bhagam? Mantras are related to yaga. Krama Parayanam, recitation done in arithmetic progression—1-2, 2-3 etc. They are reciting in tandem with the Desikar utsavam.

We are later told by Ramanan Bhattacharya(no less) that what we see here is nothing, Thiruvahindrapuram is the place to be. Conversations are had, a schedule is found, sent, and recommendations for when/how to go are shared!

Sundara Vinayaka’s Brahmotsavam ul-purappadu was an uneventful affair. A few ladies from the neighbourhood are there. Unclear what the pusari officiating knew or could do. Rani Madam sitting and reciting Potri with the ladies and something similar during the purappadu. But the ther they have for the inside rituals is super cute.

Vinayaka pandal hopping. Most were closed, only saw the Vaithikuppam Beach and Ambedkar St ones. Both are run and organised by young boys of the neighbourhood. It was surprisingly wholesome to see these boys invested in putting up the pandals.

notes.title: Conversation with Natarajan Periyavar
body: Missed It

Went to Kamakshi Amman in the morning to try to salvage the error of missing Vishwakarma Jayanti yesterday! Some notes gathered [and placed on the ritual calendar document] after speaking to Periyavar:
The Vishwakarma Jayanti did happen on Sep 17 – we missed it. It was the classic abhishekam-alankaram-deeparadhanai for Vishwabrahma and Gayatri.
Dr. Shankaradevi was there as well, and spoke of the history and origin of the Vishwakarma community. This was followed by a meeting among members, possibly about the Kumbhabhishekam proceedings.

Periyavar goes on to tell us about Dr. Shankaradevi’s maternal grandfather, Subburaya Chettiar, owner of Valli Vilas, who was the one that made Periyavar join the Tevaram Pathasala in Cuddalore, and eventually appointed him at this temple.
The afternoon and evening were reserved for visits by MLAs and the CM.

We observed today’s conversation to again demonstrate the recurring pattern of people or institutions placing themselves within a broader network, as seen with Periyavar rattling off Chettiar names and familial connections and how he was groomed by them.

notes.title: Vinayaka Pandal Visits
body: The last of our morning Vinayaka Pandal visits was to the one at the very end of Vanniar St, one block from the seashore. We are told that it is the oldest pandal of town, 47 years old. This year they have Vinayaka in gym-going demon-slaying form, called by everyone the “Six-pack Vinayakar”. And indeed not only Vinayaka, but the demon and the not-so-little Mushika all display a most chiselled physique. At the pandal, we find two boys playing with a small clay Vinayaka, applying vibhuti and kumkumam on Him. Reminds us of playing with choppu sets.

We reflect on how these are ways in which the neighbourhood supports and brings up its children, even if nobody from the neighbourhood is always present. It seems, and one indeed hopes so, that these events have the effect of firmly grounding and rooting the kids. Not just by bringing the neighbourhood together, but by giving the boys a focal point in religion – albeit with plenty of liberty to adapt the deity to the boys’ own natures and inclinations. It remains nonetheless a distinct connection of the boys with the religious and cultural tradition. The total cost of Vinayaka is based on footage (2000/- we heard?).

The Vinayaka pandals and the journey of pujas and rituals outward from temples to streets is much thanks to Bal Gangadhar Tilak. We had some thoughts about how the temple would have been the centre of social and economic life back in the day. How values emanated from the temple, shaped the social life around it, and came back to the temple as positive donations.

Some thoughts on how the Vinayaka pandals today are quite excessive in scale, and not always aware of the ecological impact of their decisions and practices. Some thoughts also on the aesthetics of these “mega” Vinayakas, and the lack of meaning and cultural context in the veneration of these.

notes.title: A Sealed Chamber and 30rs to Vaikuntham
notes.occasion: Desikar Utsavam Day 7; Purattasi First Saturday Thanga Kavacham
body: Desikar Patrikai reveals vidaiyatri from 23rd to 27th.
Perumal had thirumanjanam at 5am. The temple is very crowded. The winding path to and out of the sannathi has been flanked by barricades. A quick darshan is available for just 30rs!

The Maniyakkarar, when asked about the book on temples of Pondy, reveals some history about a room/hall beneath the main Perumal idol which he's heard has been used for storing statues during times of crisis. The passage to it was apparently sealed entirely in 2018.

Thought: the nitya-presence of adhyapakas and its significance – observing how their presence affects the impression of devotees leaving the temple after seeing Perumal; they leave a temple thats’ enlivened by chants, not bare and stagnant.

During Mangalasasanam, Thathacharya asks Deepa di not to recite the Purusha Suktam along. Yikes. One of the adhyapaka’s wives, a lady who’s always around, notices this and comes later to offer commiserations. Sounds like the age-old issues of gender and purity etc. haven’t yet found a happy balance.

Pm — Desikar veethi purappadu. I go at 630, but it is clearly delayed. I had to park a block away near Vedapuriswara Koyil due to traffic. The purappadu leaves only around 725, and soon after comes the heaviest downpour Pondy has seen in a long time. The atmosphere is surreal. I rounded the corner as Desikar began to glide forward. Calm chants of OM Namo Venkateshaya echoed across the streets from the temple speakers. The thavil and nadaswaram were faintly audible, and Desikar in gold and red glided out and forward. It was a surreal, palpable emergence. The rain picked up as he rounded the first corner, but there was no question of abandoning the procession. The call of duty was stronger than the wind and rain. An air of inspiration was about.
AM Arun went by: Nothing new at Perumal koyil today; regular desikar sevai and ul-purappadu.

notes.title: Conversation with Venkatesa Archakar
body: Met and spoke with Venkatesa Gurukkal at Lawspet. He has been at this temple for 22 years now and is the senior-most priest there. We enquire about their ritual year and get a more or less complete ritual calendar. Some inteteresting pointers from him which need to be further looked into:

list: Monthly special pujas are also known as “Erupadi”?
The Vedapuriswara Koyil Palliyarai Swami is Sokkanathar?
The Pradosha Nayakar murti is also called “Kaatchikuduttha Nayakar”?

body: After speaking, we also view the Uccikala puja done to the Sphatika Lingam. The little crystalline Lingam is given a simple abhishekam, with the highlight of annabhishekam. The Lingam is covered in cooked rice and shown deepam.

notes.title: The Ruby Robed Poet’s Rathnangi Sevai
body: It felt as though we were called to Thiruvanthipuram. We’d been thinking, watching an evening’s purappadu at the Perumal koyil, that our work would benefit from seeing these same utsavams carried out at other temples, when we found ourselves in a knot formed by the temple Bhattacharya, a staunch temple devotee named Venadavaradan, and Rajagopal Thathacharya. What you see here, they all said in more words or fewer but with equal urgency and enthusiasm, compares little to what happens at Thiruvanthipuram. Go there. Details about the Desikar utsavam there were elaborated; images of a stately procession up and down a hillside conjured. The Devanathaswamy patrikai was fished out of gushing streams of temple-related Whatsapp chats. Driving distances by various modes of transport were computed, for our benefit. The directive couldn’t have been clearer. We had to go to Thiruvandipuram.

The town we saw on the morning of September 22, the last and crowning day of the Desikar Utsavam, was a town breathed with new life. It was our first visit to the temple-town of Thiruvahindrapuram. Having been dropped on the Northern face of the complex, it was a short walk to the corridor that leads to the east-facing Perumal. We passed the Manavala Mamunigal shrine which we were not too surprised to find located definitively outside the temple complex. [The Desikar shrine, as we would soon find out, is located within the temple complex in a manner that seems to place it as though in front of the Mamunigal shrine outside.] We walked up the corridor where our notice was immediately drawn upwards by the 74 steps that ascend the mountain to the shrine of the luminous Hayagriva where Vedanta Desika himself addressed this lord who is “the basis of all knowledge”. Our attention though is quickly pulled down and back towards the primary entrance of the Devanathaswamy shrine by the sounds that emanated from there. Stepping down and in through the modest doorway, we were as though washed over by the sounds that echoed across the mandapa. An ocean of adhyapakas, learned men, seated before the Desikar shrine spilling out into the mandapa and prakara, sang the Thiruppavai, Thirupalliezhuchi and Panniru Naamam and Thiru Chinnamaalai to the revered Vedantacharya. This collective offering gave the sacred a tangible presence within those walls, and the intensity pulled even the entire being of a bystander into a one-pointed surrender. This recitation ended on the highest of notes, before Desikar proceeded on his procession up the hill. The Acharya emerged from his shrine a little past 615am. He was ruby-robed and regal for his rathnangi sevai. His gait was slow, measured, supreme. He walked not to the rhythms of the thavil, but as the very essential pulse upon which the thavil, the nadaswaram, the parayanam, the fanning, and even the devotional surrender of one’s heart all built up and moved. Before him, in a small palanquin, we noticed the utsava murti of Hayagrivar that was said to have been given to Desikar by Garuda himself. With the palanquin leading the way, Desikar proceeded around the temple, past the Thayar shrine in the south-west corner, exiting the temple through the eastern entrance corridor. He slowly made his way around the Southern face of the complex, and just as we had, he went past the Manavala Mamunigal shrine whose doors remained sealed. The Hayagrivar palanquin marched ahead a little quicker and began its ascent up the stairs, even as Desikar still dallied round the north-east corner to the accompaniment of mallari vadyam, reared also throughout by the sounds of the Vedas.

The sky was diffused and the morning cool from the rains of the previous evening. The stairs were wet in some areas, but did not prevent the palanquin from quickly covering the flight. Atop the hill Hayagrivar went straight into the chambers of Lakshmi-Hayagrivar. Desikar meanwhile began his joyous climb up the hill with the thronging of over a hundred devotees around him. Once at the top, he was met with an array of fruits, flowers and deepams by the representative priests of Hayagriva. Vedanta Desikar went into the ardhamandapam for a few intimate moments with his beloved Lord, before coming out and placing himself in the large opposing mandapam, always facing the horse-headed One. The adhyapakas lined up on either side of the divine corridor for another session of intense, immersive recitations of Vedanta Desika’s sanskrit compositions. With these it was not merely the hall, rather one’s entire being which was filled with the reverberating verses, ascending to a summit where the power, beauty and infinite fullness of God didn’t seem far. They concluded with the magnificent Hayagriva Stotram after which everybody present was served prasadam: laddu, kesari, mysore-pak and fruit. A short aradhanai signalled the conclusion of the Acharya’s annual visit to Hayagriva. “It was past 9am when the Acharya made his way to the Devanathanatha Swamy Sannidhi for the second of the Mangalasasanam. As he got down the hill, one of the Kainkaryaparas signalled to the Nadaswaram artistes to play the Nottuswaram and till the time Vedantha Desikar would start listening to the Prabhandham and Stotram in front of the Devanathaswamy Sannidhi, these artistes presented a devotional display of Muthuswami Dikshitar's English Notes.” [Prabhu S, PR Traveller blog]

Descending first, the Hayagriva murti of the Devanatha shrine made swift work of the flight of steps, retreating to Perumal’s sanctum. Vedanta Desikar followed, stopping every now and then for an aradhanai and a word of caution for his descent, “Swami Eccarikai!”. Once down, the sannathis of Perumal, Ramar, Cakratthazhvar, Thayar, Rajagopala, Andal, Nammazhvar and finally Ramanujar, were all offered Mangalasasanam by the Acharya. This was the primary event of the day, and took close to five hours of continuous recitation moving from shrine to shrine. Every shrine bestowed Acharya with fruits and flower garlands,

Acharya also receives garlands of specific flowers from each of these shrines: [Panneer roses from Hayagriva, Maniranjitham from Perumal, Pink lotus blossoms from Thayar, Jasmine from Rajagopalan in the lovely old mandapam, Kanakambaram from Andal, Magizham from either Perialvar or Nammalvar, Vetchipoo from Bhashyakara/Ramanujar]. It was close to 230pm when Desikar finally returned to his sannathi.

As the curtain is drawn over Vedanta Desika to prepare for his veethipurappadu, all adhyapakas and participant reciters are granted a much-needed break and given a serving of warm, nourishing, ghee-dripping kesari and peanut pakodas. The inertia is not allowed to build for long as the Acharya is placed inside the magnificent palanquin and brought out with the powerful cries of the sripada group. His carriage is immense to say the least, and the might of the sripadas’ shoulders lifting it is all the more so. The presence of Vedanta Desika is once again supreme and lofty by the force that upholds his movement from below. This devotional might seems to come at cost though, since we find many of the sripadas’ shoulders and traps bulged and deformed by the enormous burden placed upon them over the years. A few of the priests also have this though much more diminished, perhaps from their early years of service. The procession heads quickly out from the eastern entrance, passing the gateway to the Gadilam river, and heads out to the first of the two streets that run down the south of the temple. A dozen adhyapakas lead the way singing Prabandham. The palanquin follows at an adequate distance behind. Another dozen crown the rear with the magnificent sounds of the Veda. Thus moves the palanquin through the temple’s madaveethi, which doesn’t go as much around the temple as around the entire town! – that is perhaps an exaggeration; but it is unique given that the temple is situated on the Southern end of the town and that the procession moves entirely North of the temple through a chunk of the town. As it turns onto the other nameless street that leads directly to eastern temple entrance, the palanquin is brought in through the towering gates of the Desikar Thirumaligai, the abode of Desikar where he dwelt seven centuries ago. There now stands a 14-pillared hall constructed in honour of the Acharya about 200 years back. The palanquin is placed for a while in a mandapam at the end, while the priests collect water from the well situated in the garden outside at the back. Desikar is said to have built this well by hand, using unevenly shaped bricks. All the while within the hall the adhyapakas form two rows on either side of the palanquin each simultaneously reciting the Divya Prabandham and the Veda respectively. The sound is rather disharmonious, as remarks Prabhu. Upon completion, priests with the well-water pots marched ahead, with the palanquin troupe following behind in the same order.
It was 330pm, we left.

notes.title: Desikar Rears from the Front
notes.occasion: Desikar Utsavam Day 10, Varadaraja Perumal and Desikar Ethir Sevai
body: We returned to Varadaraja Perumal after a long day at Thiruvahindrapuram. Desikar here was also dressed in studded stone, and also carried pavitrams hanging at his base. He stood before Perumal outside the Mahamandapam, awaiting His emergence. Perumal arrived soon alongside Sridevi and Bhudevi, and Desikar led the purappadu – or rather reared it? – all the while facing his Lord.

On the third round, one of the devotees carrying Perumal reached out to me saying: “Look! Perumal is sweating! Get a close up picture!” And so I did, and indeed Perumal’s whole face was covered in unnumbered droplets.

notes.title: A Most Gracious Pradosha Nayakar
body: We go for Pradosham not expecting much from this little temple. But the abhishekam begins with a beautiful Alingana Uma-Chandrashekhara murti who stand on a Nandi utsavamurti. It is surely one of the most gracious Pradosha Nayakar murtis we have seen. We relish every second of the abhishekam. The whole temple’s ambience is much more pleasant than other days, and we wonder whether it is just the magnificent utsavar who made it so for us.
The Vinayaka utsavamurti is also on the floor, still donning the Unjal Utsavam alankaram from 20th September.
We later go upstairs to take pictures of the gopuram and vimanas.

notes.title: One More of Six Annual Nataraja Abhishekam Days
body: Today is one of the 6 annual Nataraja Abhishekams, this one thithi-based. Here are the full 6:

list: Aani – Uthiram (Uttara Phalguni nakshatra, the day of the Aani Thirumanjanam)

body: Of these Arudra Darisanam and Aani Thirumanjanam are the most prominent, but the others get marked well, too, typically with a Nataraja abhishekam and puja.

At the Sivan Koyil, the procedure is interrupted just slightly by a parallel Guru puja happening for Narasimhamunaiyaraiyar Nayanar. We saw the Maniyakarar and one of the regulars in the bhaktar sabhai (whom I will later meet working at a petrol pump as an attendant) take the Narasimhamunaiyaraiyar Nayanar utsavar out on a full inside circumambulation, going into the garba griha for a moment when the lights are turned completely off. The Maniyakarar sings, the statue exits and returns to the Nayanmar utsava mandapa. We see this happening often at the temple, with the Bhaktar group almost acting in parallel to the main temple, and being sometimes quite unconcerned with that may be happening in the garba griha.
The lights go out at Sundara Vinayaka Koyil, and while that makes the proceedings harder for the priest, it results in surprisingly stunning photographs using just the plain old phone flashlight.

Nandhikeswara has no Nataraja, but the Narttana Nandi stands in and receives as usual a most stunning and elaborate abhishekam. Its high point was the red pomegranate juice flowing over the body of the dancing Nandi. The substances are all poured in a precise, narrow stream from the conch, giving the sacred bath its rejuvenating characteristic.

The Chetty Koyil also has its Nataraja abhishekam, but with no ubhayakarar this time so the Nirvagam head stands in, and hardly anyone else is present, But a small homam is on, and the process completes in much the same way we saw it in full in Chitra masam.

notes.occasion: Purattasi Chaturdashi, First Friday of Tamil Month
body: Today’s Schedule
From the whiteboard: Maalai 6.00 Manikku Mahalakshmi Pooja, Deepaaradhanai

Anantha Vratha Nonbu (அனந்த விரத நோன்பு) is an observance dedicated to Sri Anantha Padmanabha, a form of Lord Vishnu reclining on the serpent Anantha (Adishesha). It is also known as Anantha Vratham or Anantha Chaturdashi Vratham, undertaken to seek divine protection, relief from difficulties, prosperity and family well-being. Usually falls in Bhadrapada Shukla Chaturdashi.

notes.title: Vedanta Desika on the Two Seas
body: It is the second Saturday of Purattasi, and the temple is thronging. When I reach the temple around 730pm, Desikar was on the first round of his ul-purappadu. He was rounding the north-eastern corner at the Anjaneyar Sannathi, which seemed to take an eternity. The procession was slow, perhaps deliberately, perhaps due to the crowd. Either way, whenever Desikar did move a few steps, he was sailing over a sea of people, much like the street procession last week.

I go home and return later in the night to find Desikar on his unjal. He was carried earlier by a sea of people, and is carried now by a sea of music. The unjal is on the northern prakara, right outside his sanctum, facing East. Facing him, a little distance away, is a troupe of musicians, with a Veena at the centre. The music is electric, and reaches consummation at the end of a jugalbandi by the percussionists. It is a beautiful closing to the Desikar Utsavam, before the final Panaka Puja tomorrow.

notes.title: Learning Flower Tossing
body: AM: Rama abhishekam, alankaram, Deeparadhanai
PM: 4pm Satyanarayana puja and Amman abhishekam

We spent the day at the Kannika Parameswari temple, would be one way to describe the day. We were there early, for the 730am Rama abhishekam that we’d seen announced and that the Iyer had told us about. Purattasi Sani (Purattasi Saturday), after all, so His presence must be marked. The silais themselves, four together with Hanuman, are utterly beautiful–delicate features and holding bows whose curvatures match in fluid lines the more regal postures of the figures and the straightness of their arrows. The Iyer recites almost the whole Vishnu Sahasranamam while bathing them, and he’s the only priest we know who speaks each first line of each Mantra Pushpam verse, not just the first and last verses as most tend to do, prior to the conclusion of the puja. It is an unhurried, but quick affair. Not many are around, except the morning’s ubhayakaras, a few other devotees, and us. Prasadam is a simple chakkarai pongal, aval uppma (which is delicious), and panchamritam. The lady beside me remarks: “that’s aval uppma.” I nod, because I know. “Oh you know?” she says. I nod again because my mouth is full, and after I’ve swallowed: “We make it at home, too,” I offer, “though at the temple it’s always tastier, I don’t know how.” The lady laughs. “That’s the effect of worship,” she says. I nod again, because I cannot deny the magic.

Were it not for her we may not have returned just today for the 4pm Satyanarayana puja, which happens every Pournami. But “come,” she said, and so we did. The same lady was not herself present, though others we’ve by now grown accustomed to meeting at this temple are. The women are always immensely kind, and the men less forthcoming but no less hospitable. We’ve not been allowed to leave the temple without partaking of prasadam, on many an occasion.

The puja consists of a short vinayaka invocation, followed by a quick abhishekam of what we can only describe as mini-murtis, then a navagraha puja (the temple has a navagraha shrine at the back, but the grahas are invoked in a grid of 9 thonais filled with flowers on a table next to the altar). We come in (fashionably late) when this is going on.

Another elderly lady sits beside me. She has brought damana, marikozhunthu. She insists that the dhavana be placed on the body of Vishnu, and hands it forward. “It’s special for Him from yesterday,” she insists. “Why?” I ask her, “because of Friday puja?” “No!” she answers incredulously. “Because it’s Purattasi, pournami…” When I remark that it is beautiful, she corrects me sharply. “Beautiful or not, it’s necessary,” and I’m struck by the way in which the ideas central to the Damanotsavam remain like this, fixities of practice, important, but lost from their moorings.

The priest then recites the Purusha Suktam, though in a manner I don’t fully follow, and then Ashtottaram. This is followed by a reading of the five chapters of the Satyanarayana Katha. After each one, the Iyer pauses, breaks a coconut, and Satyanarayana vrata podi prasadam (which Arun later describes as ‘powdery deliciousness’).

The puja rituals at this temple are often followed by a group of devotees, mostly women but not only them, sitting in rows on either side of the main sannathi, with two stainless steel plates: one piled with loose flowers, the other on which to pile flowers. Pink arali, usually (oleander), tulasi, chrysanthemum, small roses. As the priest recites, the flowers move, one by one. This is a standard practice, almost every time we’ve been there.

A basket in front keeps the unused flowers. As women join the puja, plates and some flowers are given to them. Some bring more, to replenish the basket used by all. Still, one can’t go too fast, as I clearly do. Sasikala laughs and chides me, while replenishing my dwindling stock with some of her own. “Go slowly!” she says, “The Ashttotara is yet to come!” I become younger in this moment, someone to teach because I clearly don’t know. The ladies demo how I must hold my hands, on which lap, how to make sure each handful has a little tulasi, a little akshatam, what to do with the offered flowers once the puja is over. And suddenly under this collective tutelage I realize that there is a pace to prayer which everyone keeps, even when they cannot hear what the priest is reciting. The movement of flowers is a page-turning or a taalam-keeping, it’s a rhythm which everyone there knows to join, and which makes, even in the absence of the usual nadaswaram and percussion cues, a cadence of its own kind.

We sit for prasadam, and I’m joking with the ladies beside me who are pulling out dabbas in which to take the food home, that I never manage to remember boxes. But this is dinner now, at 630pm, and eating early is good. “Yes!” says the woman in turquoise, repeating a formula, “before 7!”

There is still bustle in the temple because the priest must now move on to the Ambal abhishekam, and everyone is conscious of time. But we leave to make it home in time for the call with Manish about how we plan to get all this together on our new website.
AM, Rama Abhishekam

Rama in the morning is a glorious sight to behold – brilliant like the rising sun. He and Lakshmana have elegantly fashioned ear-do’s that are long and swirling, and as Deepa di remarks, give the impression of a lock of hair. The abhishekam is simple yet whole in its own capacity. There was no apparent rush or corner-cutting.
PM, Satyanarayana Puja

We are asked to join in the pushparchanai and are handed a plate and some flowers. Deepa di is offered immediately, but for me – a boy dressed in shirt-pant – the ladies are unsure and seek clarification from Deepa di!! After a yes from us both, I am handed the same. The puja is already going on, and I start placing flowers one by one. The rhythm of the archanai was not immediately distinct – there was no audible marker I could find, but a subtle pulse permeating the hall slowly grew clearer.

The image of Gurukkals tossing flowers as we have seen multiple times now floated in my mind, and I sought to replicate it. This began a series of experimental flower-tosses trying to find a balance between the flicks of the wrist and fingers. Some flowers fell back onto my lap and some went flying way over the plate. Eventually: holding the flower by the stem with thumb-middle-ring, leading the movement with the wrist until the forearm could twist no more, simultaneously bringing the palm to face upwards, and flicking with the fingers at the very last moment beyond which the wrist would hurt from the twist – I found the perfectly tossiest toss. And my goodness did it really feel like a toss. This toss paired with a concentrated sense of giving, surrender, offering – both positive and negative – of the thoughts that arose gave the entire archanai a very intimate sense of ‘rightful action’. That what was being performed there was of legitimate value and in its rightful place.
I was plucking and tossing individual leaves from the tulsi stems to make my quota last the entire duration.
I had not even noticed the little Narayana figures (two of them, one flat, one 3-dimensional) on the platform covered by the alankaram flowers.
