notes.title: A Chaturthi with Gomathi Masi
body: Sita Venkateswar’s mother is in town, and she and a friend (Veda) accompany me first to the Vedapuriswara Koyil where there’s an abhishekam to the Polla Vinayaka going on, presumably to makr this day, and then to the Kannika Parameswari monthly Sankatahara Chaturthi Abhishekam, which I’ve never seen. It is a simple, soulful affair. Just the Ubhayakaras and a few others present, a very congenial atmosphere with the Kannika Iyer of course doing it all. I saw the Velli Kavacham go on Vinayaka for the first time, and it was grand (even if the pieces did make him seem somewhat rhinoceros like!). The photos speak for themselves. The vettrilai malai and the banana malai are unusual – I’m told this is offered for those who have very specific wishes.
From the whiteboard: Sangatahara Chaturthi Maalai 6.30 Bala Vinayagarukku Abhishekam, Deepaaradhanai.

notes.title: Rites for the Dearly Beloved
body: We went in the morning to see the private pujas of those who are honoring their ancestors–this is Sarva Pitru Amavasya, dedicated to honoring and seeking the blessings of departed ancestors, marking the final day of Pitru Paksha. Several such were happening on the steps of the kulam at the back of the temple, with of course just a tonne of plastic waste everywhere (which I started collecting and soon had a big bagful, and there was more to go but I didn’t want to be reaching into people’s puja areas just to get them all). Apparently Kalyana Sundara Gurukkal pointed out my plastic picking as a model of exemplary service to the cleaning ladies in attendance.

We are told about a Marwadi practice of Lakshmi Puja that happens on this day in the evening, but we aren’t there to see it. It is true that there are many visibly non-Tamil devotees who come and do their own abishekams to the Sivalinga that is beside the naga prathistha. They count among the migrant populations that have made Pondicherry home, and who seek to find their spaces of worship in the public monuments that are here, too.

notes.title: An Unjal Utsavam Like No Other
body: Angalamman’s monthly Amavasya Unjal Utsavams are of known importance and assuredly pull great crowds. On the auspicious night of Mahalaya when the goddess descends into her great worldly abode – maha-aalayam – it becomes an occasion for greater celebrations. Across the hall, beyond the throng of devotees, Angalamman swings on the unjal; though not alone. She sits to the far left, and on the far right, with her Kiridam tilted right, sits the Vaishnava poetess-goddess Andal. In between the two, bridging the Saiva-Vaishnava split of the goddesses, is Harihara – Vishnu and Siva.

A performance of folk song with the pumbai drum distinguishes tonight from other regular Amavasyas. The singing is conversational much like it was on the day of Vallala Kottai, although it seems more structured than that. The singers stay on the topic of the deities’ stories and don’t interlace them with colloquialisms. It seems to be done more meaningfully rather than purely entertainingly.

notes.title: A Special Amavasya Samadhi Abhishekam
body: This is an important Amavasya for Nandikeswara – the temple does a samadhi abhishekam for the “piranda dinam” or birth day of Nadu Shanmuga Velayuda Swamigal, followed by an annadanam. We could not attend, but Dewan Kandappa sent photos which we have used by permission here. (From the whatsapp chat Saturday October 10 morning).

In the morning, there is abhishekam for Vinayaka, Swami, Ambal, then Parashakti (all of which happen in a jiffy, as I am there before and by the time I (Arun) return a short while later they’re all done). There was also an Anjaneyar Puja done by a lady who apparently works at Auroform (we see her entering there later). She tells me that performing this puja has been on her mind for the last fifteen years, and was able to materialise only today. Fifteen years is a long time for circumstances to align, but she says, “it is His wish and His decision; and look at how fortunate that it finally comes together on the first day of Navaratri.”
In the evening, there is the Parashakti ul-purappadu: bringing her to the Golu mandapam in the north east corner, where she will stay for the next nine days.

notes.title: A Slow Start to a Full-Tilt 10 Days
body: The schedule for the day indicates early morning abhishekams for several deities (see below), but none happen early at all. I (Arun) am around for a while, and nothing is going on. Not sure when it did get done.

In the evening, in the Yagashala, the Sri Maha Vidya Lalita Tripurasundari Homam is being performed by Arjun Gurukkal who was there for the Brahmotsavam in Vaikasi, and the other IFP scholar-priest who was there for the Ekadasha Rudrabhishekam in Chithirai. The homam consists of flowers in all aspects – the kalashams are decorated with flowers, with lotuses for every kalasham. There is an additional basket filled with flowers along with the usual dravyam-filled baskets. The homa kundam has flowers marking all directions. Parashakti ul-purappadu – stopping by Yaga Sala as they perform the purnahuti for the homam and offer deeparadhanai and flowers to the goddess.
The Day’s Schedule:
7AM - There is an abhishekam for Kashi Viswanatha (sponsored by the Siruthonda Nayanar Sabhai), and later also for Vinayaka, Swami, Ambal, then Parashakti. Alangaram on Visalakshi is Rajamatangi
PM - Durga Puja with aradhanai and viniyogam.

notes.title: Starting Navaratri Before the Sri Vaishnava Navaratri
body: We go after 9pm. Dance in the makeshift mandapam outside, invoking the Dashavataras. Temple doors only left slightly ajar as everything closes down inside. We are called for the final closing prasadam – warm milk and ghee-laden kesari. The dancer groups outside, along with their own utsavar alangaram and pujas which go on daily, have no formal connection with the Perumal temple as such. This is all organized by “Hindu Munnani” says Prasanna, though the signs say it’s VHP. Some of the performances are very good.

We go at 9pm when the temple is on the verge of closing. The lights begin to go off as we stand there, the moola Ambal has her curtain drawn and Sriram Gurukkal briskly walks multiples times around the Pecchayiamman-Madurai Veeran shrines with lemons in hand – perhaps a closing rite involving a mouna vratham which we have not observed before? Angalamman is right there in her alankara mandapam, today in the form of Meenakshi – the same alankaram as Nandikeswara’s. Behind her we notice the Ardhanareeswara murti, which turns out to be the same murti used yesterday for the Harihara alankaram on the Amavasya Unjal.

We go a little before 9, and temple is rather empty. There is a dance program going on outside on a makeshift stage. Inside a Golu has been set up. It is very elaborate with Ambal on the central top-most step with a mala or prabhavali of peacock feathers, garlanded with jasmin. On either side of her are Katavarayan and Siva-Parvati respectively, below whom extend the two rich arrays of Golu bommais. There are a lot of Krishnas! Almost a whole few padis of them. And some swanky modern dwellings sit at the very base.

notes.title: A Balayalam Navaratri for Kamakshi Amman
body: Since the Kamakshi Amman Koyil has done its Balayalam, no major festivities or utsavas will take place. Navaratri is therefore not marked this year with any degree of grandeur, but is marked only by daily abhishekams and aradhanais in the evenings. There’s a patrikai posted outside the temple with the daily schedule and the names of the Ubhayakaras.

notes.title: Maravalli Meenakshi
body: We follow the alankaram-making from 11am upto its completion around 2pm. Amman is given the form of Meenakshi today. The utsava murti is the core, around which additional bronze limbs are added as extensions, and the rest of the body is skilfully enlarged and shaped with newspaper and rope. The original utsava murti is hidden entirely by the torso of the now enlarged Meenakshi. Her head is not crafted with newspaper, but with banana plantain stalk instead – “Vaazha Mattai” as they say. These are cut to size and layered to provide thickness. The body is then draped in a saree, meticulously passing though the legs and around the back multiple times as required. Maavu is then prepared with maravalli kalangu – tappiocca flour, mixed with green paint and water to create the dough that is to be Meenakshi Amman’s face. The priest applies the maavu to the plantain stalk and within a few moulds and presses of his finger, there emerges a beautifully proportionate face. His fingers move with a sculptor’s adeptness and the rough shape of the face is ready within minutes. The rest of the hour is spent in detailing the nose, lips and eyes. Another hour after that goes into painting the cheeks, lips and eyes, placing the crown, bejewelling the deity and adding any final touches before the evening puja. At the end of this long afternoon, only the flower-garland is left to be placed, which will be brought fresh just before the evening puja.

In the evening, we meet Dewan Kandappa at the temple as we reach after the aradhanai is over. He explains that his wish is not merely to have entertainment during Navaratri, as many other temples do (Chetty, Ghousiga; Perumal remains loftily above the arts programme happening at his doorstep but not in his name– done by the Hindu Munani/VHP), but to grow arts traditions. For Navaratri there should be musicians playing all instruments, but they either charge too much to come or simply dance with a CD playing. All of it being too much or insufficient, Nandikeswara keeps only a golu and no performances.

notes.title: Sri Vaishnava Navaratri Starts a Day Later Than Everyone Else’s
body: Perumal Koyil starts Navaratri on Dwitiya, unlike everyone else–we cannot figure out why, since amavasya (associated with pitru karma) is long over by the time of sunrise. We reach Perumal Koyil just as He leaves from the garba griha–alone, hand resting on his gada or mace, noticeably without Sridevi and Bhudevi as he is about to go have his annual time with Thayar. 3 times pradakshina, and then Perumal is taken backwards to his seat beside Thayar, in her sannadhi. Door closes for what feels like an eternity. It opens to a long deeparadhanai and sodasha upachara. It is by now after 8pm, so we leave to make sure we get to other temples on time (have been out since 530pm, temples close at 9 or so), so we plan a return by 9.

When we come back, the puja in Thayar sannadhi is finishing. No sevai, no adhyapakas around. Perumal has a big bunch of damana in his hand though–a sight that makes us laugh, as that’s a sign of Kamadeva on him, just as he’s come to see Thayar. Are people just not telling us what they know about this plant and what it represents? Are they assuming we know already and don’t need telling because it’s a matter of some shyness? Anyway, the door closes again, and opens with Perumal robed in a veil and damana knocked out of his hands and left with Thayar. Aiyo! The veil, we’re told, is to cover His shyness after having spent this time with Thayar. So there is this human-humorous dimension to Sri Vaishnava practice, too. He goes around the back of his own shrine (can’t circumambulate Thayar) and then back to his asanam – position in the garba griha. Done for the day!

notes.title: Dwitiya’s Tritayam at the Sivan Koyil
body: There are three things going on at the Sivan Koyil when we enter at 830am: the yagashala homam (Sri Mahavidya Tripura Sundari homam, being done by Arjun Gurukkal who officiated at the Vaikasi Brahmotsavam and another who is a scholar at IFP), a Durga puja (abhishekam and alankara done before we get there, prasadam viniyogam/distribution about to start), and a Gopuja.

Morning kaalam homam has Damana in a basket which they offer to the kalasams. We are intrigued by this presence of Damana for the Tripurasundari Homam, trying to make connections of the Kama story relevance here. But we are told by Arjun Gurukkal that they used Damana only because there was spare, not because of ritual prescription or necessity. There is a lot of spare damanam around this time of year, as we are soon to find.

The Durga puja is being done by the Bhaktar sabhai, if the yellow sign that usually signals their events is any indication. Ladies are in a crowd doing their chanting. The morning’s event is followed daily in the evening by a puja and further parayanam. Yesterday, the group was in the maha mandapa, many in the day’s colour (orange), and somewhat unconcerned with the Parashakti purappadu when it happened.

Next, Gopuja. There is a lady who comes to the Sivan Koyil daily to do a trishathi puja– 300 holy names (Trishati) of Tripura Sundari. For the 9 navaratri days, the daily early morning ubhayam for the temple’s Gopuja is also hers. The IFP priest is the one who performs the Gopuja, and it is a brief affair. Cows are anointed with a paste of chandanam, and turmeric, kunkuma dotted on top. Two round smears on the two sides of the rear, along the back and tail. (The priest asks me to do the smearing, and shows me how when I ask but he presumes I will know already–at my age, I’m expected to have seen many such pujas already.) Cow and her calf are draped with fabric, puja begins for Mahalakshmi (always at the back, never ahead of the cow where her older sister Moodevi sits), the lady sponsoring does 3 pradakshinas around both cow and calf, one at a time, flower on the cow’s rear, a basket of fruit is brought out and offered (the cows get to eat from it later, very tenderly offered and fed), lamps are waved. And that’s pretty much done.
There is a steady stream of devotees into the garba griha, we notice golu bommais in the ardha mandapa with Parashakti–though this is her mandapa, exclusively. More devotional incursions?

On the way out, Arasoo Mama passes by on his scooter looking most un-Arasoo mama like in a striped shirt, and he talks about the importance of this puja being done daily–Siva has a bull after all, his keeping one is a sign of his protection of the herding traditions. In the past cows and bulls were just kept, he said, long past their ages of utility. Then came the British and the merchant men, who said: why, why not utilize. When the utilitarian logic came in is where the troubles began. Traditions of using leather for instruments were from cows and bulls who died naturally. Pujas are meant to use only dry wood, dry coconuts – no difficulty to anyone, hands folded. But if we once had more cows per number of people, now those numbers are stilted, space is lost, agrarian customs are lost, and a commercial mindset prevails. Now there appears no option other than slaughter.
Oh, and the alankaram for Visalakshi today is Kamakshi!
From the whiteboard: 12.10.26 Navarathri Thingatkizhamai
Kaalai 9.30 Manikku Swami - Ampaalukku Abhishekam Nadaiperum. Ubayathaarar: Thiru. UCO Bank Oozhiyaargal
Maalai 4.30 Manikku Mel Durgai-kku Sirappu Abhishekam Matrum Deepaaradhanai Nadaiperum. Ubayathaarar: Thiru. Nesal Srinivasan Kudumbasthinar

Around 8pm, there are two lines of ladies sitting outside the utsava mandapam, watching the puja. In the main sannadhi mandapa, men are doling out prasadam on plates in anticipation of the puja getting over. The priests make some time for women to sing. Then the Navaratri puja continues with kunkuma archanai. There will be a deeparadhanai after and of course the viniyogam though we don’t stay for that. Perumal calls, and we don’t want to miss his emergence from Thayar’s chamber!

We go at 530, only to find the Parashakti (Thaiyal Nayaki, actually, Vaidiswara’s consort) abhishekam mostly over. Not sure how elaborate this was, no signs of fruits or milk even, though the priest helper asks me to take the bowl of chandanam over to the moolasthanam–so we know they’ve used it for sure. Parashakti sits in a shrine to the left of the golu, which occupies the right half of this long utsava mandapam. She’s given a gold kavacham, there’s a very quick puja for her and the Thani Ambal who sits in the middle of the golu arrangement. All done in 15 mins or so, while the dancers and singers for today’s performance are getting set up on the stage just outside. Ghousiga has performances like these outside, all Navaratri days.

830pm and the utsava mandapa doors are not yet open. Tharakkara neram thaan, one lady says, it’s the time when they open. Puja inside the moolastanam is as much to the lamps as it is to the deity, who is shrouded in dhoopam smoke but decorated with row upon row of simple flower malas, floor to ceiling almost. The utsva mandapam, when it does open next, has what is a Durga Alankaram.

The priest’s plate brought around for the devotees to touch with hands before puja is a bowl of red kunkuma plus…. damanam again, tossed on her while the priests chant their mantras. How is this merely a coincidence of season and nothing more? There seems to be quite an excess of damanam around today.

notes.title: Tavaloka Yoga Nidra
body: She is in Tavakola alankara today–a yoga nidra posture of penance, meditation, peace. Her face has been made in blue, eyes closed, a bright checked sari to match. We’d stopped in earlier to see the building of her form, but ducked out to get other work done and somewhat regretted it when we went back in the evening to see her in finished form–utterly beautiful, with a yellow and blue flower mala. The priests had asked for vadamalli to match her sari better, but they got this instead which perfectly matched her face. The puja was as usual a dramatic event, perfectly choreographed. Both brothers sang after, and recited the Kamakshi ashtakam (so there is some Sanskrit that comes in after all).
(This was the day we went with Riddhi Shah, who tagged along with us to Ghousiga, Sundara Vinayaka, and here).

notes.title: Malas of Devotees
body: Velli Kavacham for the main murti (following abhishekam), utsava murti sitting alongside, deeparadhanai. In the evening, Ambal is in Durga-like form, with parijatam malas that have been hand-made by the woman sitting now and making pink arali malas, and white vetchi poo tucked in behind her ears. The Iyer tells me he has done the alankara himself, maybe with the help of another priest called in–he starts at 2, has to finish by the time of the evening pujas, then finally undo the alankaram and prepare the temple for the next morning’s abhishekam. He’s not done before 11pm, and is up again in the temple by 6. These are long, difficult days for the priests, especially those without added helpers. In the evening, too, women are gathered and both them and their children are standing to tell stories of the Goddess.
From the whiteboard: Navarathri 2-aam Naal
Kaalai 7.30 Manikku Ammanukku Abhishekam Deepaaradhanai
Maalai 6.00 Manikku Uthsavar Ammanukku Sri Lalitha Sahasranama Kumkuma Archanai, Kanni Pooja, Shodashi Deepaaradhanai

630ish, coming from Ghousiga, we see Sundara Vinayaka with a golu set-up and about to start puja. Ravinder Sir is about to do an abhishekam to Durga, the Sivan in the main sannadhi and the moolamurti Vinayaka. Presumably after this will be the Navaratri parayanam and puja. A handful of ladies are around as usual, setting things up.

notes.title: A Much Understated Amman
body: Kannan sir who did all the Aadi masam alankaram sent me photos of Navaratri day 1, so we went on day 2 to understand this temple’s Navaratri traditions. Simple and understated. But Draupadi amman’s utsava form stands in her gold kavacham in the Golu mandapam which is where the utsavas are all usually kept. The Kavacham looks best in the ther festival, the priest says, and he plans to change her attire a few times in this period. Moolamurti meantime is in orange, with a vettiver mala creating an angular shape behind.

Vedapuriswara Koyil would have done a Murugan abhishekam today along with the morning Swami Ambal and Durga abhishekams. We note that things for the Navaratri time are apparently very driven by bhaktas/ubhayakaras. If they will it, it happens, otherwise the temple as such does not undertake the full length of festivity.

notes.title: Getting the Lawspet Alankara Lineup
body: Short visit here, to see the golu, Durga alankara (as Varahi today). The priest gave us the alankara lineup:

list: Weds, will be something in the Perumal amsam, says the priest.
Thursday: Shiva Linga Puja, with one hand bent gracefully downwards
Friday: Mahalakshmi (See the entry for Oct 17 for details)

body: To make time for the alangaram and to allow it to dry and then be visible to devotees all day, the priest does the abhishekam early at 6am. Pulls the screen and does the alankara himself or his son does – it’s quite impressive, painted. He tells me how he does it is a “rahasyam” like the Chidambara rahasya.

We stop by the Bala Mutthumariamman temple which is locked because the same gurukkal tends to that also. This temple is unique for having both the small head of Mariamman and the Parashakti figure behind her in black stone.
An Annadanam will happen at the temple at 11am today, as it always does on Tuesdays.

(from the chalk board) 3-aam Naal / 13.10.26 Chevvaikizhamai, Chevvaai Pagal 11 Mani "Annadhaanam" Nadaiperum Maalai 7.30 Mani Golu Mandapa Deepaaradhanai Nadaiperum.Ubhayadhaarar: Sivathiru Satchithanandam Avl, Thirumathi Thamarai Avl, IllasuppettaiNavarathri Alangaram "Sri Vaaraahi Amman"

notes.title: Late Birds Get the Scoop
body: Reach here when all is done and dusted! But this means quiet time with the deity, and the priests. We’re asking about this detail or that, and the priest mentions the Balatripurasundari temple – Oh, is that where the Melmalayanoor Angalamman stays when she comes for Masi Magam? We ask – and he replies that that practice isn’t at all ancient, it’s just from a few years ago and is largely a monetary exercise. What he says is continued by another man (devotee) present who explains how it feels to go to that temple, when it is so focused on money. Another woman comes by and says: I thought you must be talking about Tirupati since I head “kaasu koyil”! But they affirm that temples in Pondicherry are generally not this way, and that you can go to most of them without hesitation. Manakkula Vinayaka used to be very bad, they say. Someone who worked there would put some long tweezer-like apparatus into the hundi and get money out all the time. He’s gone, so the problem is gone, but the damage done to the temple and its reputation–well, that stays. In general, temples here don’t function this way.
There’s also some talk about how the renovations were done for the Mutthumariamman koyil, and how they changed many things but never the main sannadhi which still retains its old uneven stone floor.

The take-home for us was that some of these integrative traditions may not be so old at all, and that some (though not all) are driven by modern monetary concerns. Angalamman temples in general seem to be plagued by this? The conflict between the town Angalamman and the one in Angalanagar which we’re following was over money collection issues in the main market area, too.

notes.title: Mohini Alankara on Tritiya
body: Day 3 Alankara is Mohini – reclining, eyes half closed. We watch the form-making, which the priest is not happy with so he undoes and redoes it before we come back for the face-making, which we document fully. Lots of talk today about body proportions, how to bring them about, what shape of face with what posture works best, and so on. Face colour was achieved with kesari colour today! The regular tints etc. are not satisfying. Ambal remained more visible and therefore more present in the alankara process today, thanks to the side-leaning posture of Mohini:”Aadhara shakti aa nikkaraa, Ambal” said the priest.

Video of Meenakshi alankara went up today, too. Thought of including the priests’ names in the view as they are the ones doing the alankaram. But remembered Arasoo mama from the Vedapuriswara koyil. I asked him one of those Adi Fridays when Ambal is all decked up in chandana kaapu alankaram, who had done this beautiful alankaram. But he replied, while going down the aisle with the kunkumam: "when you ask a question like that, we will always say that 'we have done it.'" Authority and attribution just work very differently in temple spaces. One tends to attribute the only authority to the Divine presence there–He called me so I came, She told me how to wrap this thread, He gives me guidance to make this alankara. This transferral makes common acknowledgements focused on the individual and his or her specific skills or achievements ill-fitting, and even problematic.

We saw this on the early morning of day 5, when the morning temple-opening rituals were going on – mainly jala abhishekam, and changing the vastrams. notes.title: Ganesha Alingana Shakti
body: It’s Navaratri Chaturti, therefore today’s alankaram is Ganesha Alingana Shakti (गणेश आलिङ्गन शक्ति) or “the Śakti who embraces Ganesha.”

We spent 8 long hours with barely a break for lunch and a quick tea in between to watch the Nandhikeswara priests Sivavijay and Sivakadhir create this form. They had already prepared the form of Ganesha using a metal frame, covering it to create the required body and trunk shape with thengai naar (coconut fibre). All this was held together by jute string, and then a surface smoothened with the aid of a little plaster of paris (because it dries quickly and it allows them to keep and re-use the form). On top of this Ganesa is chandana-kaappu, which is then painted. The PoP inside allows for a degree of moisture-absorption, so the process is smooth. Ambal’s form is given more with the use of pre-prepped cloth-covered limbs (with their brass hand and foot “endings”), and then enlarged with newspaper. She is then dressed in a sari, with jewels and malas while Her face is done and the body of her son. Hands and feet are eventually done with maravalli maavu (tapioca flour) as that is less “wet” and easier to work with than chandanam. The priest does the Ambal’s face with chandanam at first, and then discards it entirely because it does not dry fast enough (no PoP beneath, only banana stem and pattai pieces), and hangs and droops and distorts. He repeats the process with maravalli kizhangu maavu.

At the end, shaping hands and feet also with maavu was a little rushed – closing in on 5pm and the aradhanai starts at 630pm. The flower malas go on top– a few in woolen colours, one with the fresh flowers just arrived. We leave to go home and change, but when we’re back we realize the priest’s search for perfection has brought about a more angular draping of the malas, which makes a huge difference. “By that one korai (lack or deficiency), the whole form should not be tarnished,” he would say, and re-do what he felt not to be correctly done, or formed. Everything took longer because of it, but everything was richer and more perfect because of it.

Caught the end of the evening puja cycle. Sankaranayarana Chettiyar said: “you both are so busy running temple to temple, you never come here any more! Panchami so you’re here, and you don’t know what you’re missing!” He understood our predicament perfectly, and is such a kind man in spite of all the many dynamics he clearly has to manage all the time. Puja to Kalatheeswarar was just over, Ambal puja happened, then we went over to Parashakti in her golu mandapam where the process repeated (curtain opens to a short aradhanai, curtain closes for prasadam etc., curtain opens again for more lamps, archanai basket brought around, puja happens, then the final aradhanai and kunkumam distribution).
Same kunkuma archanai navaratri puja going on. Alangaram today is Annapurni.

Mahalakshmi Alankara second day, when we see it. Seems like the alankaras are kept for 3 days each (Durga, Lakshmi, Saraswati), and only the malas changed daily. The moola sannadhi is decorated with fresh flowers, the utsavar is in a Gajalakshmi form. Brass lotus below, two elephants poised on the tall kutthu vilakkus on either side. Here the puja is mainly the aradhanai, which follows the usual sequence of lamps – the mahadeepam or Aḍukkut dīpam first, then several decorative others, then the plates with wicks that look like cigars (yikes), followed by the kumbha deepam. In this, we see Jnanavel swami picking petals and propitiating the lamps rather more than others at other temples. It’s beautiful, no doubt, but different.

Curtain closes, prasadam offered, curtain opens, archanai happens and everyone gets to touch the flower basket that’s brought by, short puja, nakshatra deepam aradhanai – and then of course the kunkuma distribution.

Today’s Alangaram is Ardhanariswara, for Navaratri Panchami. We hadn’t planned to be there the whole day but once we got there, there was no leaving – something about the process by which this form was built pretty much out of the cloth-formed limbs and then banana stem pieces – banana stem “pattai” or flat pieces or the stem core “thandu” pieces – was so mesmerising, we couldn’t bring ourselves to leave. The process also went well, in the sense that the priests got the proportions right from the start and didn’t have much undoing and redoing (but for the arms which were originally tied to the frame and brought out front more later, so that they didn’t seem like they were growing from the back of the body). The whole form was then covered with maravalli kizhangu maavu, tapioca flour, made in two colours: blue for Uma, a mustard yellow for Siva, பச்சை நீரம் and செந்நீரம், said the priest, green and red-hued. The colours made for some fine photos and videography. Having filled my phone (again), I switched to camera videos which were so much more alluring I wished I’d done this from the very start. Arun’s been taking on camera from the get-go (smart). Then the face was shaped and body was painted over – what an alankaram this was. The inspiration: Ardhanariswara from Thiruchengode, who is shown holding a sengol in exactly the way he is in the alankara. Sivavijay said he always wanted to go to this temple, but had never had the fortune to go.

Thiruchengode is a hilltop temple, a padal petra sthalam on the Salem-Erode National Highway. Sambandar’s திருக்கொடிமாடச் செங்குன்றூர்/ Thirukodimaada Chengunrur (old name for Thiruchengode like “Senthi Nagar” is a name for Thiruchendur) His hymn “Venthaven Neeraninthu” describes the Lord wearing sacred ash and having the Goddess as one half of his body.

One story: The rishi Bhrngi was an ardent devotee of Siva, but he refused to worship Parvati. In some versions of the story, he transformed himself into a bee or a small insect and attempted to circle Śiva alone, even when Siva and Parvati were seated together. Parvati, displeased that her own divinity was being excluded, sought to become inseparable from Siva. In the familiar account, Siva granted her a place as half of his body, revealing the Ardhanariswara form. The legend conveys an important theological point: the Goddess cannot be separated from Siva, because Sakti is intrinsic to Siva himself. The temple's own sthala purana includes the tradition of Bhrngi's worship.
Not much different here than the last few days. Ambal in a different sari, 2 dolls placed in the golu mandapam by a devotee who came to pray for a good marriage.

Kunkuma kaappu for the moola murti today. Mixed only with panneer or scented rose water, said the priest. It got a little brown though, should have been a bright red. Perhaps the commercial panneer water had some acidic or alkaline properties that interfered?

notes.title: A Private Golu Mandapam
body: We have kind permission to share private golu photos from the home of Shankaranarayanan and Madhavi, whom we know from years ago, and whom we’ve seen among the Ubhayakaras at the Sivan Koyil. They keep a large golu at their house on Eswaran Koyil street! Many pieces which they proudly show, collected by his grandmother and then his mother. Lovely sets, including Ravana sabha, vilakku puja, even the Abhirami bhattar story. I forget how many padis, but it well near went up to the ceiling. Beneath was green turf and so many more pieces, of lesser importance, but many personally irreplaceable beadwork pieces made by his mother. My golu at home is absolutely nothing in comparison! The green turf should have been mud brought from outside but who does that sort of thing any more? (I overhear them saying). It makes me think that golu practices themselves must be changing so much, and must have become far less ritualized and embedded in local ecologies.

notes.title: Sivan Koyil Cooking & Kaasu for Kasi Visalakshi
body: So much going on here!

Abhishekam and alangaram in the main sannadhis. Lots of crowd there. Saw a woman in full black burkha today, face flap open, she had probably come with friends. I caught her eye and smiled. She reciprocated. Wonder what her impression of the temple was.

Durga puja and parayanam by a group of women. There are a few groups, clearly. This is one. They also do the parayanam in the main mandapam at times. Another goes over to the Kashi Viswanathar sannadhi – that’s a separate group, I think associated with the Siruthonda Sabhai (who also do Nayanmar related pujas every Sunday). Today’s alankaram had her in green. While the group chanted, the priest threw flowers… Lalitamma came and pulled me down to sit. It was so sweet. Then she told me I could learn music and sing, too, it’s never too late. I was laughing. Indeed. And then we chanted the Mahishasura mardhini stotram together. Very cute. She’s such a small-figured lovely person with an incredible voice.
Mahalakshmi sannadhi: a small group, and the Goddess bedecked.
Not much more than an aradhanai for Murugan today, it being sashti! The sannadhi was even locked.

Kashi Viswanathar and Visalakshi, today dressed as Mahalakshmi: another group getting ready to do parayanam, and the Goddess all dressed up in … kaasu, money. It was strangely attractive, and certainly creative. The source of riches, after all. But a little literal? Mutthumariamman also had a bowl with cash flowing out in a mala form, which felt a little too literal. Some men were stringing crisp new Rs 10 notes in a long mala they were going to hang from that sannadhi’s vimanam to where, I’m not sure. We left before we could find out.

Of course the Homam going on in the yagashala, with Arasoo mama at the helm and the ubhayakara the lady who does the Trishati archana daily, plus the Navaratri Gopuja. She’s doing her bit to carry the temple, it appears!

body: Went early morning 6am for the Durga abhishekam. Temple slowly waking up. Ramanan Gurukkal also was there, but not doing much. All sannadhis open, including the lovely Shanmukha who sits in front of a mirror not so he can see himself, but so you can see his 6 heads, including the ones at his back). Venkatesa Gurukkal (the older priest) was directing the younger priest with the stutter doing the abhishekam, which was just jalam and paal. The “gundu gurukkal” (koncham gundaa iruppare? Said the priest aid) would do the alankara later, maybe starting at 8am. He wasn’t there yet in any case. Moolamurti abhishekam about to happen, but not in a major way.
The alangaram lineup:... Varahi (Tuesday, when we went), Mahalakshmi (Wednesday), Santana Lakshmi* (Thursday), Gajalakshmi (Friday), Annapoorni (Today)

*Santana Lakshmi (also spelled Santanalakshmi) is one of the Ashta Lakshmis—the eight divine manifestations of the Hindu goddess Lakshmi, who collectively preside over different forms of wealth and prosperity. Santan (or Santana) translates to "progeny" or "offspring". Thus, Santana Lakshmi represents the wealth of children, family continuity, and the protection of future generations. But the alankaram didn’t have 6 arms, as Santanalakshmi does - and the Murugan koyil didn’t put baby Skanda on her lap? (says Arun). It does seem somewhat odd. Maybe we got the name wrong.

Next stop: Chetty koil, where the Palliezhucchi has already happened, and also Swami abhishekam. Ambal looked like she was waiting for one. JayaShankar Gurukkal at the main sannadhi, another priest at Ambal’s. Gurukkal told us that this business of bringing Ambal from the palliarai was started only a few years ago by a bhaktar, that usually there’s no such practice (I mentioned that the Sivan Koyil does this on Mondays, and he said “oh” and nodded). Anyway, he continued, there is no need, Ambal remains in the palliyarai. For utsavams it’s Chandrasekara and Uma who go out. The Ambal figure who is always just outside the sannadhi is Nilayambal or the “Ambal who stays in the Nilayam (house)” sort-of-thing, also called Bhoga shakti. The palliyarai swami sits opposite her, on a pedestal.

notes.title: The Last Purattasi Saturday
body: We went next to Perumal – it’s the last Saturday of Purattasi, and the last of his major alangarams. Moolasthanam just opening. Hanuman in a cute embroidered green suit. Wondering now when the Maa Munigal Utsavam will begin, and what it will be like compared to all the others … Sekar mama has told us that while the Desikar Utsavam is largely upheld by Iyengars, the Maamunigal Utsavam is done by Naidoos, which makes them each qualitatively different utsavams.

notes.title: Early Morning at Ghousiga
body: Finally: Ghousiga: Morning opening movements here, too. Thulasi Mariamman priest doing the rounds at the back, milk and water mostly; we caught him doing the abhishekam to the Pillaiyar, Vishnu, and Siva lingam (Vaidyanatha swami). Another man was pouring water on the other murtis. Prep. for a big abhishekam to the moola murti was going on; fruits being cut and all. But they were waiting for the Ubhayakara. How are there sponsors for the early morning awakening abhishekam/pujas? It was barely 8am when we decided to leave.

The Sivan Koyil was abuzz–as usual. I ran up to Arasoo Mama and told him I was going to catch him again when things were more free to sing that Abhirami padhigam I love so much. He said we could take golu photos, so we did. Durga puja ends tomorrow (Monday, Navami) we were told. Visalakshi alangaram was Ardhanariswara, quite well done. Homam going on, with the main kalasham in a beautiful new blue sari with a green border–very mayil-like. The group of women from the Durga puja were at the yagasala entrance, doing one more parayanam.

This morning there would have been an abhishekam and aradhanai for Swami-Ambal, and in the evening Ambal Herself was in Chandana Kaappu. The usual 430pm Durga abhishekam, aradhanai and parayanam was over, too–probably why the group was free to sit now by the yagasala.

Following a quick stop at Varadaraja Perumal (where the shodadasha upacharam was still going on) we headed to Angalamman. Today’s alankaram was most certainly Santana Lakshmi, Arun said – money, child on lap and all. The usual fairly large group of women doing their kunkuma puja while the priest chanted. It was drizzling outside when we left.
Missed Mutthumariamman this evening, will have to go again tomorrow for her Saraswati swaroopam final day.

Kannika Parameswari utsavar alangaram today was “Veda Saraswati”: she holds a scroll & jasmine mala & rudraksha in her right hand. Tomorrow will be Saraswati proper, says the priest. Moolamurthi Vasavi Kannika has chandana kaappu today. Lamps and other items for the Sodasha deeparadhanai are all washed and looking bright and shiny. The Iyer places white chrysanthemums on each, which make them look brighter still and even lovelier. When we enter, he is doing his usual Sahasranama reading, and there’s a group of women there reading along – but independently, none of them seem to be in sync with any other.

Prityangara Kali alankaram. We followed it pretty much all day. The difference between this and other alankaras is twofold: this is a Kali alankaram to announce Ashtami, and the evening deeparadhanai was accompanied by no less than Kayilaya Vadyam which makes it quite the dramatic spectacle; and the “build” was with kalimannu or clay gathered from riverbanks and ponds usually, where it has become fine and wet and malleable. So the priests use kalimannu for the Kaali alankara, to give the largeness of the face some stability. The fearsome face emerges almost effortlessly, though Sivavijay takes his time to finesse and perfect. A blue maravalli kizhangu or tapioca flour paste is applied over top. Teeth added, eye sockets filled with bulging balls, lined red, flames painted around the face, hair spread over her shoulders. Her body is bedecked and full of all the usual allure, but the face–well the face makes you think twice, the absence of her usual lion mount notwithstanding.
Arun’s mother came for the evening Deeparadhanai.

notes.title: Pujo à Pondy
body: The Bengali community in Pondicherry–sizeable due to the presence of the Sri Aurobindo Ashram–has been celebrating Durga Puja here for several years now. It is mainly organized by the Bangabharathi (Bengali Association of Puducherry), and takes place at the at Saibaba Thirumananilayam (Sri Sai Baba Marriage Hall), located at 8th Cross Road East, Thiruvalluvar Nagar, Puducherry. We were given to believe there are now three such in town, but this one is the oldest, initiated by several women we know, including Arun’s own grandmother. The pandhal is set up on Sashti and remains until Vijayadashami; it features (sometimes very short) religious rituals like the Sondhi puja, cultural programs, music, and community meals. We made a quick halt here to get photos and take in something of this wider religious atmosphere. But we went in the morning, when hardly anyone was around and the mood was preparatory–priests readying things for the day’s rituals, men and women cutting vegetables, among others directing curious photo-takers like us to “document it well.”
PS: Pandhal is a Tamil word that has not become “Pandal” (pan like saucepan+dal) in Anglicized pronunciation. But Mandap would be the more common descriptive term.

notes.title: Everywhere You Look, Saraswati
body: Today’s alangaram at Nandhikeswara is Saraswati as today is Saraswati puja, but this alangaram is done by the old priests of the temple since they came on hard times after leaving this place so as a support and continuity for them this 9th day remains theirs. Consequently, this is a more conventional alangaram with even a paper veena.

At Kannika Parameswari: again Saraswati alangaram, Amman in gold kaappu. The temple is abuzz with kids in costumes, there’s a sort of fancy dress competition going on. The priest gestures to us to take photos of the kids, some of whom look just very adorable as little Murugans or Ganeshas with paper pink trunks. We joke about how the rains happened today so that tomorrow’s ceremonies will happen in the clear. The Iyer laughs.

Mutthumariamman: Narayanaswamy was aiding the second Muraikarar (Jnanavel swamy’s “turn” finished a day or two prior). Moola Amman was in gold kaappu, the utsavar was of course Saraswati. Same at Angalamman, Saraswati with a veena that has been fashioned out of cloth. Usual crowd of women doing kunkumarchanai, followed by a Deeparadhanai.

At Vedapuriswara Koyil, Durga was in Chandana kaappu, this is the last day of puja to her and the crowd for naivedyam was big. It was Visalakshi who became Saraswati (with an actual, beautiful wooden veena). 2nd kalam homam was going on. We’re told to return 11am tomorrow for the neyyi kulam (ghee pond) alangaram.

notes.title: Rare Visions of Reflections
body: Neyyi Kulam, or a pond of ghee. We’d seen this presentation darshanam once before, in the Draupadi Amman Koyil – a pond of ghee on a base of chakkara pongal catches the face of the Mother like a mirror, and you see it there. Except the effect there was not so evident or impressive. The Sivan Koyil, as ever, does it differently. Two large vessels of pongal went into the Ambal sannadhi. Arasoo Mama came out to say that they were low on ghee, and could we get 2kgs more from Vijaya Ganapati next door. We did. The line was already long for this darshan. When the doors opened, we realized that there’s no electric light in the garba griha, only a line of oil lamps to Ambal’s left. Wait, said Arasoo mama, I’ll take you in later. So, we waited. When the Maniyakarar and EO went in for darshan, so did we. Waited till they left, and had our moment in solitude with the great Lalita Tripurasundari.

I’m not sure what we expected to see or feel. Was it the darkness? Was it the scent of ghee and camphor? Was it the line of flickering lamps? I was deeply moved. And, indeed, there was Lalita Tripurasundari’s face visible in the neyi kulam. What was the point of seeing her there when she’s there to be seen right in front of you? But the question did not matter. Something about the clarity of that ghee surface in that light, in that closed, still, airless room. Something about seeing differently. Something about moving so that you can see only that face in only that stillness. It was like Arasoo mama had said just moments before. Mani, Mantram, the bell, the mantras, the smells, the sounds, the sights – they all converge, and when they do, in just that way, there are no words left to speak about what it is like.
Yagashala was empty and the kalashas gone, presumably taken to the moolasthanam for a final abhishekam. One lone kalasham remained, but sans a coconut. Navaratri clearly about to come to its end.

Arun went back for the Ambu event in the evening, while I was still at Nandhikeswara. Chandrasekara and Uma were coming out from the utsava mandapa, came around to the corner where the naalvar mandapam is. Guru mama did a puja to the banana plant there – took kalasham sprinkled water onto it, went to Chandrasekarar, took the ambu (a vel in this case) from his hand, and stabbed the vazhai maram a few times. Then the tree was pulled forward and made to fall down. He took a few more jabs at it once it was done – ambu returned to Sivan’s hand, and they carried on.

By the time I got there, Chandrasekara and Uma were on their way back to the utsava mandapam. Quick quick aradhanai there, and the door locked. Time for Parashakti to return, too. She came out of the golu mandapam and went back to her chamber. Golu kalachuffied. Done.

notes.title: The Gurukkal’s Dash-ami
body: Gurukkal said they were ready to do the Ambu Podudal, which properly should happen around 630pm, I learned, perhaps based on the thithi timings. It roughly did. Alankaram still going on when we reached, though moola murti was ready with ambu in hand. Once the utsavar was ready, she was brought out into the street. In the ground across the temple was a banana stem, dotted with kunkumam and chandanam. Sriram Gurukkal brought out the Kalasham from the main sannadhi, water from it was sprinkled and the area sanctified along with all of us standing there. Utsavar in the form of Durga watching. Then the elder Gurukkal went into the garba griha, pulled out the ambu and came running – running – down with it, to stab the vazhai maram and cut it down. It all was very dramatic, unexpected, and happened in a flash. The Durga utsavar circled the cut banana plant once. Then the priests and crowd went back into the temple and we left so as not to miss the event at any of the other temples we were chasing that evening. But as we did, Durga had her victory dance around the prakaram of the temple inside.

The next day we saw @yenpondy’s video on this very event, from exactly our angles and perspectives, and we did wonder how that footage had been procured without us noticing a thing–until Arun pointed out that there’d been a woman there taking video… Another instance of Yen Pondy being at every place, at every moment. Not sure how they do it. But they did capture the senior Gurukkal’s wild dash exceedingly well.

notes.title: Dashami’s Only Purappadu
body: The puja here was to start at 730pm, by the time we came there it was past 9pm so we had missed the ambu event for sure. The place was calm enough, felt like a regular Tuesday with the regular devotee crowding. We went in search of the purappadu, which we found on Bharati Street. I don’t believe any other temple did a purappadu on this night. But here was Ghousiga’s signature little red tractor was pulling the deity along. They were stopped at the doorstep of another temple (it’s courtesy or convention to do so when another deity passes by, presumably) where the ambu event was already over–we saw the “dead” banana plant across the street. We had kesari prasadam there, got photos and went on our way.
We could never get to Lawspet that evening. No purappadu there for that other Murugan temple in our set, but they would have had the ambu event just outside the temple in the street.

notes.title: The Headiest Victory of Them All
body: This place knows well how to mix ritual devotions with music, sound, and a good measure of street theater. The Kaiyala Vadyam was on in full swing when we reached, and the deity was being brought out of the garba griha. This time Siddheswari’s own face and the classic temple alangaram, with Her seated on a lion, bow in her hand, trishulam by her side, which is itself dressed in a small sari like she is the Goddess in miniature form, and with jasmine malas. Banana plants tied everywhere as decorations. Very festive atmosphere, like street theatre about to begin. And what theatre it was.

The Dewan later sent out a message on Whatsapp that said this among other things: “Vijayadashami marks the occasion when the Goddess, through her gracious and merciful gaze, destroys from their very roots the five great inner afflictions within us: kāma (desire), krodha (anger), lobha (selfishness or greed), mada (pride or arrogance), and mātsarya (jealousy or envy).” So, there were 5 arrows which the priest held in a flower-strung bow, and he held it and stood in front of the Goddess, and swayed to the beats of the vadyam or the nadaswaram, which played alternatingly, and then took each arrow (ambu) in turn towards the hapless, waiting banana plant and stabbed it with it. Durga moved from left to right twice in this process. Two arrows from the right, two from the left, and the last from the right again. Then the banana plant is cut, once, twice, with a large knife. The other priest comes over and pours red kunkumam over it, and we cannot tell whether it’s Mahisasura’s blood or the Goddess’ blessing. Sivavijay swami now brings the trishulam that’s been beside the goddess all along, and plunges it into the cut, almost flat surface of the plant. The dress and decorations are removed, and a short abhishekam is done right there, to the ambu. The ambu is returned to the Goddess, she circles the abhishekam table where the fallen tree lies, and she is carried once again indoors and there a victory dance happens. The nadaswaram plays, Kailayavadyam beats, sambrani smoke fills the air, and the priests throw red rose petals, yellow chrysanthemum petals, and whole flowers in the air over her. There’s so much it must be cleared quickly away. What a scene, what a heady sense of victory they manage to create.

notes.title: A Time to Propitiate Bhavani Amman
body: Saw the end of the 5pm Abhishekam to the Bhavani Amman, after which there would have been a Navaratri puja. Usually Durga gets an abhishekam and alankara. The group of women who assemble here sing, then an arati is done to the golu with a “Jaya Jaya Shakti” song set to the tune of “Jaya Jagadisha hare.” It is usually a quiet neighborhood-like atmosphere and affair.

notes.title: A Small Event to Mark a Great One
body: I found my way to Draupadi amman where the ambu poduthal had just finished – I was late. If I had any doubts, the men seated there affirmed it: “You are too late!” they said, in chorus. But by the looks of it, however, it was just a small affair. The next day was another neyi kulam alangaram, Rangaradjou swami said, but we couldn’t make it to that.

notes.title: Kannika’s Ambu Event
body: We’d checked on the start to this puja a couple of times. The first time (on the way to Angalamman), we saw the Iyer doing his usual Sahasranama prayanam to the utsavar, who was ready and waiting on the side prakaram, in front of the Kuberan yantra, instead of her usual spot just outside the garba griha. The second time we passed by on the way to Nandhikeswara, it seemed like they were getting ready, but not yet there. When Arun finally got there after Nandhikeswara, the banana plant had just barely come down, Kannika Parameswari was facing it (standing on the road facing west). She then moved in a long circle up into the middle of MG Road, and then U-turned back into the temple. She was carried around the whole prakaram once, and brought back in through the main door. Then, of course, her victory dance! Arun left soon after that started so as to be at the Sivan Koyil in time.

notes.title: The Vel in Jnanavel Swamy’s Charge
body: We didn’t think we’d make it here in time for the Ambu Poduthal (அம்பு போடுதல்), but delighted to arrive and find the puja barely starting, following the usual movements, much like in the other temples. It’s not Jnanavel Swamy’s charge of the temple these 15 days, but he was there nonetheless, as he is traditionally given this task. He brought the spear out with a focused and purposeful look, dashed towards the plant, stabbed it, moved back and repeated the process thrice. On the third time, he slit the banana plant down the middle. The tree was cut and made to fall. The Vel was returned to the deity. We left soon after as there was no sign of a purappadu here or any movement outside, to try to catch Ghousiga’s Murugan also in the act.
*Technically, the ambu is an arrow–but most temples have a spear or a trishulam in the place of arrows, or they use both as with Nandhikeswara.

notes.title: Over Before We Know It
body: Today was the last day of the Vaishnava Navaratri utsavam, and we thought we’d not miss the ambu poduthal here for sure – but boy were we wrong. The patrikai said 7pm, but for some reason nobody could fathom, Ramanan Bhattacharya decided to finish it off at 530pm, so by 6 they were all done. The cut banana plant was in the corner by the mirror and the Alvar sannadhis. Perumal had done a 3-round ul-purappadu looking very grand on a golden horse with a new kireetam which looked a little like a jaunty little hat. It was new, we learned, so Arun was deputed to take photos of it, and the objects in Perumal’s hands. The alankaram was kept in the maha mandapam. We stayed for prasadam since there was not much besides we could do anyway. Many people complained that they’d missed the evening’s event, so it wasn’t just us. It was entirely unlike the priests to do something so early and without warning.

Incidentally, this is the only temple that had some Vanni Maram (Prosopis cineraria) branches around, along with the banana plant. The ritual is frequently performed near a Vanni tree because the Pandavas once hid their divine weapons in a Vanni tree during their exile, so the tree becomes a symbol of their victory. Some people were also collecting the twigs “from the spot where the arrow landed” (or close enough anyway) as a charm bringing good luck, prosperity, and protection.

notes.title: Navaratri Continues Here When It Has Ended Elsewhere
body: We went to Kannika after a longish day of working out illustration integration with Abhishek, and working on Sthalam’s website. Had a long chat with the Iyer, who was as usual affable and kind. I’ve updated Kannika Parameswari’s ritual calendar with further details. As usual, there was a new alangaram for the utsavar, and Ambal in full Chandana kaappu with 3 heads, mirroring the utsavar–a Muppidari form, or mumukha, I don’t recall which. The Iyer was explaining what we do to others around, and it was warming to hear him affirm our efforts. He’s a kind soul.

The day after Navaratri is Ananta Sayana, he said, for this temple–a rest day. After this, in this temple’s tradition the Vidaiyatri continues a full 7 days. This makes Kannika Parameswari’s Navaratri celebration a 17 day vizha, which pretty much no other temple does. The printed patrikai posted by the door affirms this, along with providing a schedule for various competitions and community events.

Bit of an adventure here. I got myself dropped at Lawspet Murugan temple for Pradosham. A group of women belonging to the Durga Mandali (100 members or so, said Ramanan Gurukkal) were there taking the sankalpam. The lamps and other dravyangal for the abhishekams were getting prepared, largely by a pretty young woman in a pink kurta. I noticed because I’d never seen a woman doing that work in a big(ish) temple before. The utsavar was in the Sivan shrine, and that Pradosha murti was beautiful, so I went over to take photos, knowing well that by the time the abhishekam started, I’d not be able to get any view of him at all. Then was speaking for some time to Ramanan gurukkal about lamps. Here are the names he gave me:

list: The maha deepam is also called an adukku arati. It has layers of 5, 7, 9, 11 etc places for wicks. It is also called the alangara deepam.
There are deepams also named by the number of wicks they hold: Ottha deepam, Retta deepam, Moonru deepam etc.

Then there are the ones with the specific figures or vahanas in front: Rishabha deepam (with a vrushabha in front), Purusha deepam, Naga deepam, Mayura deepam, Sēval (cockerel flag) deepam. There can also be simha and gaja deepams, in different temple traditions.
The plate deepams are called Pancha thattu.

body: Ramanan Gurukkal seemed to suggest there is an element of alankara to the deeparadhanai, but I’m not sure I understood him well enough. Deeparadhana is ordinarily a form of upacāra (உபசாரம், ritual service or offering), not a form of alankaram.

Before the puja starts, Raghavan Iyer (the main priest’s son) comes over and asks about our photography–long story short, he’s never asked us about why we were here before, his father was always aware though, but now he says that someone from the Nirvagam called and asked about my taking photos because there are/have been temple thefts. I promise to wait and talk to the Special Officer, Mr Selvaraj. Once Arun comes, and the pradosham abhishekams are over, we rush home to get my UHCL card so I can make a formal introduction to Selvaraj Sir. We wait until after the Pradosha puja is over and do exactly this. He is a kind man. We explain the project, he asks a few questions, and then visibly tells Raghavan Iyer that we’re good to go. Phew.

There are several abhishekams today, by the way – because Ambal gets one, too, as do both the Nandis outside each of their sannadhis, along with Pradosha nayakar. Siva’s nandi gets a velli kavacham, the gold is reserved for Sivan himself. Ambal has some parts of gold kavacham but not full.

The pradosham itself is a simple, soulful affair. 3 rounds of ul-purappadu, one to music, one to the Iyer’s Sanskrit chanting, one to Periyapuranam, Thiruvasagam and Potri recitations by all present. Someone hands out the script for these, so people walk around and read it together, not always in complete harmonization, but it creates a nice atmosphere no doubt. I took photos and made a PDF of the sheets.

Once the three pradakshinas were done, the Pradosha murti stopped on the south-west corner, where Venkatesa Gurukkal spoke briefly about “upcoming events” – what a nice idea, to keep people informed that way. He spoke about the pandhakaal muhurtam though for what reason I’m not sure (lots of interfering noise), about the annabhishekam upcoming, gomata puja on pournami, which happens to be the same day, and asked for people to bring vegetables for the special alankaram, including long snake gourds because they resemble serpents. (Sivan in vegetal alankaram!)

Prasadam is sundal, sweet puttu, and a kalanda sadam. We speak for some time to Dandapani sir, who is the one who sings Tevaram, Thiruvasagam etc. at each puja. He tells us that the two Murugan sannadhis at the back contain figures that were the original moola murtis of this temple. Vinayaka came first–therefore he is Adi Vinayaka–then the small Muruga and then the one seated on a peacock – but the Mayilam mathadhipati came and said that the moola murti should be standing to give blessings to all, not seated. So they installed the present Murugan. He spoke at length about his devotion, about having a swelling on his foot, having a dream like experience in which an elder man came into his house with the door all flung open at the deepest of night, rapped him thrice on the foot and told him he would be fine. And he was. Like this many “Adhisayam”-ana experiences.

He also talked about the utsava murtis. The temple has two, one for the Thirukalyanam, and one who is exclusively a Samhara murti, who is present only for the Soora Samharam. These things keep changing, he said, by kaalakattam (period, era). Different people come in different kaalakattam, as the Nayanmars did, each preaching, teaching, adjusting, modifying, continuing, discontinuing–and the temples bear the impressions of all these influences.

notes.title: Atmartha Lingam Pradosham
body: Pradosham happens here also to the Atmarta Lingam that is in one corner, near the Ramar Sannadhi. The lingam has a beautiful Vasuki form over it, with red beads hanging one from each head. The alangaram today was Annapurni, seated cross-legged with a bowl in one hand and a spoon in another, and moola Kannika was in full chandana kaappu with what seemed like flared skirts. It was quite stunning even from the outside to see this. There was a large group of women doing singing and parayanam today. The day’s kolam was as usual outside the moola sthanam.

notes.title: Annabhisheka Vizha Day 1
body: I caught but a glimpse of this pre-puja in between dishes to Chetty Koyil and back to Angalamman for the Annabhishekam (which was undone by the time we reached there anyway, so it wasn’t worth the dash but who knew?). The yagashala was locked, but there was a mandala on the surface usually used for kalashas, the homa kunda was still smoking, flowers by it were fresh still, as was the cooked rice on four corners always placed there towards the end of a homam. Some older kalashas were in front facing east, but to the north were the relevant ones, it seemed. Nothing much seemed to have been done for Vinayaka (the patrikai mentioned a Vigneswara puja, see below), but the queue to the garba griha was mighty long. I peered in while passing by the Nandi, from a point where one can get a view–and it seemed that the place was lit only by oil lamps, so looked mysterious and alluring even from afar. I couldn't stop, but I did wonder what Sivan looked like inside there, in that beautiful, smoky, dark chamber of His.
Published Patrikai Schedule: Aippaci mācam 8-ām tēti — 25.10.2026 — Tirumuṟai: Sunday, 6pm

notes.title: Two Misses in a Go for Angalamman’s Annabhishekam
body: We had designs of focusing on Angalamman for the Annabhishekam as the only other significant abhishekam we’ve seen here has been the Theipirai Ashtami Kali Abhishekam and we’ve never seen the Sivalingam here worshipped, but clearly the Goddess had other plans for us. Patrikai time was 7pm, and we were undoubtedly late, but hopeful that this temple had been slightly delayed–but no, abhishekam was done, saris screens pulled while alankaram was going on. Okay, we thought, at least we can see the annabhisheka-alankaram. Rather than wait, however, Arun went home for a quick poori dinner and I did my runs to Chetty and Sivan Koyils. We reached back almost at the same time, a bare 40 minutes later – only to find it was all done, and the screens were up again, but not for the annabhishekam, more for the final alankaram and deeparadhanai. So disappointing! These weren’t even kept visible for a half hour, as they were at Chetty or Nandhikeswara. It was a lovely scene though, with mostly women and children in attendance, everyone in a neatly tied sari, and no pushing, rushing, everyone making room for everyone else (I love this town and these temples). Vasanth who runs the Angalamman Instagram page promised to send me photos, so at least a “digi-darshan” may be possible, though I shall have to pursue him for them as I’m yet to send him Navaratri photos myself (sheepish emoji here, but not like I have not been over-my-head busy!).

The puja itself was a simple one, prasadam was the kalachified annam turned into curd rice, and served with a side of what looked like sambar-rice. Handed out by Sriram Gurukkal and a helper who looked rather worse for the day’s wear. I cannot imagine how they manage all the work, and shepherd the crowds, and still manage to keep their composure at all times (but for scolding some rowdy kids here and there).

notes.title: Two Non-Starters at Lawspet
body: Too much rain this morning, so we skipped the Gomata puja that happens every pournami. Evening we went at 545pm and the prep for abhishekam was just going on. Some lovely yellow flowers laid out on a plate, which the priest said was thanga arali–a wild plant, take a little of it and you will see vaikuntham, he said. That poisonous. We left intending to return, but never could with the rain and all the temples doing their annabhishekams at the same time.
Schedule:
10am, Gomata Puja, this apparently happens every Pournami.
5pm, Aippasi Pournami Annabhishekam for Sivan

notes.title: An Annabhisheka Vizha Like None Other
body: “We’re biased towards Nandhikeswara,” Arun declares. He couldn’t be more right, but for the fact that he didn’t add “unapologetically so.” It is possible that the more learned men are still primarily associated with the Vedapuriswara and Perumal Koyils, but Nandhikeswara with the stewardship of the Dewan has a rooted culture of its own, no less schooled or cultured. And the priests are just talented and skilled, as all our Navaratri videos have amply shown. Today there are not many present for the first abhishekam, which itself includes annam, cooked rice among the standard dravyangal or substances. I’m really glad we got to see that. Vrushabha has a darling garland of eggplants, the torana over the garba griha threshold is made of a raw banana bunch and other creatively hung vegetable maalas. The canopy over the moola murti is itself decorated with vegetables. Narttana Nandhi had a mala of corn and, was it ridge gourd? It’s all quite a sight to behold.

We came back once for the main Annabhisheka Alankaram, which was as with all this temple’s alankaras, spectacularly done. The lingam had been enlarged and embellished with vegetables, and the deeparadhanai was going on with the usual graceful, almost choreographed method. The photos speak volumes here, though I had nearly to crawl to get them as the crowds by now were full and thick. And oh, oh, oh, that Kailaya Vadyam again, and what it does to my beating heart!

On our third and last return for the evening, there was only a little less crowd, the annam had been removed and was set to be distributed as prasadam along with a big barrel full of all the vegetables, and the final venneer or hot water abhishekam was going on. Can’t leave Sivan sticky with rice after all. A little of the rice had been put into the temple’s well – some is supposed to go feed the running waters and the living creatures before becoming prasadam for us. We hadn’t seen this ourselves, but were told that was the method. When the last venneer chombu was poured, one last alankaram and deeparadhanai and the prasadam viniyogam began. We’re taking photos of the food on the way out, because distribution hasn’t started and we’re not waiting – and then this lovely man from the Sivan Koyil, who has seen us just about everywhere and had started out by saying to us “no photo!” comes over and gives us from his plate. I love the atmosphere in these temples, and what broadness of spirit it seems to draw out of people.

In each temple this evening there’s been rather more food distribution than usual. Abhishekam became the alankaram became the annadanam. Or, this seems to be one ritual in which the distinctions of the three are fully removed. You don’t just consume a little panchamrutam or smear yourself with a little chandanam or vibhuti, you consume the cooked rice as a meal supplemented with other annam dishes. If the distinctions matter on other occasions, today they did not. A reminder perhaps not to take them as that separate to begin with, even on other days–or to recognize today as a sort of dissolution, I’m not fully sure which.
We started out at 320pm, we got home past 9pm. What a night.

*Every pournami is marked with a special abhishekam at Sivan koyils in Kashi, says the priest. For Karthikai it’s deepam/fire, for Margazhi it’s kambali porvai (woolen blanket), in Thai masam it’s ghee and so on. But here in “Thennaadu” or the land of the south, only the Karthikai and Aippasi months’ practices hold.
Schedule Announcement from Dewan Kandappa:
On the full moon day of the Tamil month of Aippasi—Sunday, October 25th—the grand Annabhishekam (offering of cooked rice) festival for Lord Sri Siddheswarar will take place.
From 4:00 PM onwards: Thirumanjanam (sacred bath) and Annabhishekam.
From 6:30 PM onwards: Special darshan of the deity adorned with cooked rice.
From 7:00 PM onwards: A discourse by Dr. V. Sankaradevi on the topic, "The Significance of Annadhanam (offering of food) as Praised by the Nayanmars."
From 8:00 PM onwards: Removal of the rice adornment, followed by abhishekam (sacred bath) and darshan.
From 8:30 PM onwards: Distribution of anna prasadam (consecrated food).
We invite all devotees to participate and receive the divine blessings of the Lord.

notes.title: White Rice Raiments for the Kanyaka on the Night of the Full Moon
body: The whiteboard announcement said 3pm, but Pournamis are busy days at this temple–the Satyanarayana puja had wrapped up early morning, and the Ambal abhishekam was about to start. Kanyaka’s utsava murti was in the garba griha with her. What was it–the green drape on the deity, the posture of the utsavar, the light as it shone into the garba griha, the absence of any crowd or the sparse use of ingredients (dravyangal) – but this was a beautiful abhishekam. The Iyer here of course is one of few who works completely alone, and it’s a lot of work, but he seems to do it without complaint or pause or any shortcuts. When he was done he gestured to us to say that the other alankaras would be done by 5pm, so we could come back then. Kind man.

When we come back (much later than 5), indeed the atmartha lingam on the side is dressed in cooked rice as is the Kanyaka Herself–and does she look resplendent or what. A piece of yellow pumpkin is the crescent in her hair, which is topped by grapes. Two more pumpkin pieces make her ears. The folds of her garments are indicated with avarakka, beans, carrots. There are patchs of red (pomegranate?) on her abhaya mudra-extended arm. If the point of a well-done alankaram is to cause you to stare and stare and stare–this one sure did the trick. It helps that these alankaras are visible from the road outside, they just draw you in. The priest called in to do the alankaram is one we’ve seen at the Sivan Koyil, but he pays no attention to us.

Kamakshi alankaram for the continuation of the Navaratri vizha, which was on-going at the time and we couldn’t wait to see it finished. A lady there pulled us in for the deeparahanai, which we saw and quickly left for Angalamman.

notes.title: A Politician’s Annabhisheka Annadanam
body: Running between temples in the rain, we got to Chetty Koyil only after all the early abhishekams were done, and the alankara was on display. It was quite beautiful. What looked like a tiered stand was placed in front of Kalathiswara, and that was filled with cooked rice, and layered with more fruit than vegetables that had been there at other temples. There were pineapples, apples, and broken coconuts which looked especially beautiful. Looked also like there was a banana leaf at the base with some additional offering. I waited while others did their archanai pujas, and went out to the Ambal sannadhi, which looked completely bare in contrast.

In the prakaram next to the Perumal temple were rows and rows of people sitting with not the usual mandarai leaves but proper banana leaves. Ok, I thought: big annadanam here! And a lot of the Chettiars were serving–so I thought, well, that’s a bit different, maybe that’s the nature of the puja today, but no. I noticed the photographer present before I saw there was this politician in white, doing the serving along with the Chettiars. And I thought: aah! It’s that sort of event!
Kotiswarar gave us something else though, a prescription from the Kamikagama (he says, unverified): “तुलामासे पौर्णमीयुक्ते अश्विनी नक्षत्रे अन्नाभिषेकं कारयेत्॥” which means:
“In the month of Tula, when the full-moon day coincides with the Aśvinī nakṣatra, one should perform the bathing of the deity with cooked rice.”
Alrighty then.

notes.title: And the Alankara Prize of the Day Goes To…
body: Sundara Vinayaka Koyil has so far been a little neighborhood temple driven by the family’s commitment and pure goodwill and devotion, but fettered by their own personal (and budget) limitations and the sheer difficulty of running what is a full-scale set of pujas without a dedicated priestly staff. Rani Ma’am is is always the one organising, Ravinder Sir is always in the role of priest. That was the case today as well, but it felt very different. The place was full, for one, with mostly women (as usual), reading prayers and songs. It’s all a little off-key as usual, but somehow the chorus manages to sound harmonious. The abhishekam seems to have started on time at 6, because when we get there a little while after, it’s over and the milk is being handed out. Bhavani Amman outside is already washed and bedecked, so that must have happened before. Alankara for the Siva-Parvati duo is nearly done, and we can see it from a slit in the curtain, cooked white rice pressed onto the lingam and into the form of a human face, which is very strikingly done. The curtain opens, the deeparadhanai starts, the women are singing and chanting. After all the “no photo!” scares at other temples (though we’ve followed guidelines as given in every single place, and never taken photos when/of what we weren’t supposed), it was a relief to have women make way for us to actually get closer and take the photos we want. To the point of asking others to move, a little bit to our embarrassment, but such kind efforts and nobody complaining that we block their view for a bit. All that was such a relief. The women were reading as Ravinder sir was placing flowers, in much the way the priests and bhakta groups at the Sivan Koyil do. We left then for Nandhikeswara, which would have had its alankara ready and deeparadhanai starting just about then.

Temple announcement: On the occasion of 'Annabhishekam' (offering of cooked rice) at the Sundara Vinayagar Temple tomorrow, Sunday, October 25, 2026, an 'abhishekam' (sacred bath/anointing) will be performed for Arulmigu Meenakshi and Sundareswarar, followed by the offering of cooked rice and 'deeparadhana' (ritual offering of lamps) at 6:00 PM.

notes.title: Ashwini Annabhisheka Vizha
body: I don’t think I’ve seen longer lines or crowds at the temple for a darshan event. Utsavams, yes, darshan not so much. But the mandapam was full even at 530pm, and the queue snaked around the temple to the back of the Murugan shrine. We were staking out a position when we bumped into Uma mami sitting at the side entrance to the garba griha, with her usual happy disposition, talking about how Arasoo mama (Chandramouli Gurukkal, actually) advised her to be there so that when the ubhayakaras finish, she can go in that way and see the annabhishekalankaram and exit sooner than the waiting crowd. “I’m waiting here trusting Siva, and if you wait with me I know I’ll have more power,” she said. She’s always one to call us out as being to so many temples, our darshan is as powerful as any deity–hilarious.

But, tt didn’t quite happen that way. Arasoo mama came, indeed, and admitted all of us along with the ubhayakaras saying “this lady lives in the next house, these two are my neighbors, that lady lives on my street…” Also hilarious. We got in with everyone, and the temple doors opened, but we were then the closest. The Annabhisheka-alankaram was nice, but being in that space with everyone was nicer.

Soon after, once the Ambal darshan and aradhanai were done, people queued up for annadanam and prasadam – another long, long line. The hot sambar rice being given out smelled fine, but we left without it. What we’d seen had been enough.
The Vedapuriswara Koyil does this event a day after all other temples thanks to an Ashwini nakshatram calculation, while all others match their timings to the full moon thithi.
